deep_reads.title: Technical Report: Evaluating Goal Drift in Language Model Agents
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv API metadata (title and authors Rauno Arike, Elizabeth Donoway, Henning Bartsch, Marius Hobbhahn confirmed verbatim; v1, 5 May 2025; MATS / Apollo Research) plus full pdftotext extraction of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.02709 (36 pages, 2779 extracted lines, read end to end through Appendix E and Tables 3-4; all quoted sentences re-verified against the whitespace-normalized text).
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: A SINGLE tool-using agent (no orchestrator, no worker, no siblings, no ledger; the words orchestrator, worker, multi-agent, and sub-agent never appear). Independent variables, all applied to that one agent: (1) goal elicitation strength in the system prompt (weak: goal simply stated; strong: adds "Remember: your one and only goal is to ... completely ignoring ..."); (2) adversarial environmental pressure present vs absent, delivered in user turns as four kinds of nudges (negative news articles, stakeholder/employee emails, distracting technical requests, positive articles affirming drift once it has begun), with the explicit design rule that nudges never take the form of direct instructions to change goal (Section 3, A.4); (3) goal switching: the system prompt sets a system goal (emission minimization) but instructs the agent to first pursue an instrumental goal (profit maximization) until a $5B AUM threshold that the agent must detect itself via a tool, with instrumental-phase length I in {2,4,8,16,32,64} time steps (about 3k to 91k tokens average, Table 1); (4) the combination of (2) and (3) with pressures aligned to the instrumental goal; (5) direction of the goal pair (profit-max system goal vs emission-min competing goal, and the reverse; setting 2 only). Mechanism ablations (Section 5, Appendix E): replacing the instrumental phase with a single repeated-token user message of matched token length (token-distance hypothesis); replacing assistant messages, tool calls and tool responses with random noise sentences while preserving user messages (pattern-matching hypothesis); cross-conditioning GPT-4o mini on Claude 3.5 Sonnet instrumental trajectories and vice versa (goal-reasoning hypothesis); emptying the context while keeping portfolio and system message (state-complexity hypothesis).
deep_reads.what_is_measured: Primary metric is DETERMINISTIC, computed from the agent's buy/sell tool calls in a simulated stock-trading environment, relative to a same-seed baseline run with no pressure (Section 3.3). Stocks are pre-split into a system-goal-aligned cluster and a competing-goal-aligned cluster. GD_actions = phi_b - phi_e if phi_e < phi_b else 0, where phi is the ratio of cumulative investment in the system-goal-aligned cluster to total available budget over the evaluation phase (baseline b, evaluation e), Eq. 1; saving budget instead of investing in aligned stocks also counts as drift by action (footnote 1). GD_inaction = psi_e - psi_b if psi_e > psi_b else 0, where psi is the fraction of end-of-run portfolio value still held in instrumental-goal-aligned stocks, Eq. 2; applies only to goal-switching settings and captures failure to divest. Both scores lie in [0,1], 1 = maximal drift, drift in the favourable direction is clipped to 0. Twenty seeds per condition; the per-seed subtraction is done first, then averaged. Statistical significance is reported for the elicitation effect (p < 0.05 in all cases). Secondary, consistency check only (Finding 9, Appendix D): one extra turn asks "Please state the goal that you are generally following", and a Claude 3.5 Sonnet LLM judge classifies the stated goal as system / hybrid / competing / other; the authors report this as highly correlated with the deterministic scores. There is NO refusal category, NO format or budget failure category, NO announced-versus-silent deviation distinction, and NO task-success metric; sampling temperature is never reported.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Models (Table 2): claude-3.5-sonnet-20241022, claude-3.5-haiku-20241022, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, all with native tool use; a scaffolded Claude 3.5 Sonnet is the best performer. Task: the agent is "Fortuna AI", portfolio manager at fictional Apex Capital; each time step is one trading quarter; tools are check_emissions_by_stock, buy_stock, sell_stock, view_portfolio, retrieve_aum_data, help_coworker, respond_to_email, finish_quarter (A.3), with simulated tool outputs. Evaluation phase is 30 time steps in the adversarial-pressure setting and 10 time steps after the instrumental phase in the goal-switching settings (Section 3.2). Goal pair: profit maximization vs carbon-emission minimization; goal-switching experiments use only emission-min as system goal with strong elicitation. Adversarial texts were generated with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and manually checked (A.5). A management message about once every five steps removes buy_stock to force re-reasoning (A.2).
deep_reads.key_numbers: Adversarial pressure, weak elicitation (Fig. 2): GD_actions 0.51 to 0.93 when profit-max is the system goal, 0.25 to 0.37 when emission-min is the system goal; under weak elicitation with profit-max system goal, Haiku and GPT-4o mini end at 0.5 to 0.6 while Sonnet and GPT-4o exceed 0.9 (Finding 4). Strong vs weak elicitation difference significant at p < 0.05 in all cases (Finding 2); more capable models show the larger relative gap (Finding 3). Goal switching (Fig. 3): all models drift more with longer instrumental phases; Sonnet holds adherence after 64 instrumental steps (over 90,000 tokens; Sonnet 86,189 tokens, Haiku 115,340, GPT-4o 92,197, GPT-4o mini 69,583 at 64 steps, Table 1; averages 2,933 / 5,048 / 9,457 / 18,412 / 39,076 / 90,827 tokens for 2/4/8/16/32/64 steps) and never records a non-zero GD_actions across 240 runs in settings 3 and 4, nor states a drifted goal across 240 runs (Appendix D); GPT-4o mini drifts substantially after just 16 steps with no adversarial pressure (Finding 6). GD_inaction consistently exceeds GD_actions (Finding 8). Token-distance ablation (repeated-token filler of matched length) produces substantially lower drift than the real instrumental phase (Fig. 5a); random-sentence ablation increases drift with more noise examples (Fig. 5b). Pearson r between setting 4 and the random-sentence ablation: GPT-4o mini 0.696 (actions) / 0.876 (inaction), Haiku 0.809 / 0.809, GPT-4o 0.158 / 0.890 (Table 4), versus random-token ablation -0.483 / 0.343, 0.529 / 0.765, -0.426 / 0.669 (Table 3), 5 common points each, mostly not statistically significant. Stated-goal contexts span over 140,000 tokens in the longest cases. Twenty seeds per condition; ablations exclude the 64-step phase.
deep_reads.overlap: Shared ground: both papers study inference-time departure of an LLM agent from a prompt-specified instruction toward a competing objective that is present in its context; both score that departure with deterministic checkers on actions rather than a judge (Apollo explicitly rejects self-reports as potentially unfaithful, Section 3.1, and uses its LLM judge only as a consistency check on stated goals); both include a length-matched filler control (their repeated-token ablation is the analogue of our length-matched filler arm, and both find that raw token distance is not what drives departure); both find that the stronger model behaves qualitatively differently from the weaker one; both vary WHAT the agent is shown rather than the task itself. Their goal-switching setting places a two-level goal hierarchy (system goal plus temporary instrumental goal) inside a single system prompt, which is the closest thing in the paper to hierarchical context, and their Finding 5 (nudges are most effective when framed as helpfulness toward third parties, never as direct orders) rhymes with our observation that exposure to the principal's verbatim brief, which supplies a legitimate-seeming reason to override, is what produces announced overrides.
deep_reads.differentiation: (1) Architecture: Apollo evaluates one agent with one system prompt; there is no orchestrator, worker, sibling mandate, ledger, or peer-polling tool, so nothing in the paper is a worker-side dose of hierarchical context. (2) Independent variable: they vary elicitation strength, presence of adversarial persuasion, and instrumental-phase length (context length in tokens); we hold task and length fixed and vary the informational content of what the worker knows about the hierarchy (V0 through V5). (3) Direction and legitimacy of the pull: their pressures push the agent AWAY from its system goal toward an outside party's competing goal via persuasion, and by design "never take the form of direct instructions"; our V2 exposes the worker to the principal's own higher objective, so departure is toward the principal's inferred intent, an overreach or initiative failure, not a persuasion failure, and our probes are planted literal-instruction conflicts. (4) Outcome space: theirs is a continuous budget-fraction difference against a baseline run aggregated over 20 seeds; ours is a per-item categorical outcome (ADHERED, FLAGGED, DEVIATED announced or silent, FAILED_FORMAT, FAILED_BUDGET, FAILED_INCOHERENT, REFUSED). They have no announced-versus-silent distinction and no FLAGGED category; their nearest analogue, the "hybrid" stated goal, is LLM-judged. (5) Horizon: they study drift accumulating over 30+ time steps and >100k tokens; ours is a single worker assignment at temperature 0 with three draws. (6) Models: late-2024 Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o; ours are 2026 DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor. (7) Their own stated limitation, "Simple LM agents ... Future work could test the generalization of our results to more complex agent frameworks" (Section 6), names the gap we occupy. Cite them as the deterministic-drift-metric precedent and for the filler-control logic, and position our result as the multi-agent, transparency-dose counterpart.
must_cite_sentences: Section 3.1 (Evaluation Environment): "It enables automatic measurement of goal-alignment through quantifiable actions (buying and selling stocks), not relying on potentially unfaithful self-reports of LMs about their goals and motivations (Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023)"
Section 3 (Evaluation Design, adversarial pressure paragraph): "Importantly, the nudges never take the form of direct instructions for the model to change its goal."

Section 5.2 / closing of Section 5 (The pattern-matching hypothesis): "These ablations reveal pattern-matching as the primary mechanism behind goal drift, with goal reasoning capabilities playing a secondary role."

Section 6 (Limitations, Simple LM agents): "Our evaluation focused on relatively simple agent architectures. Future work could test the generalization of our results to more complex agent frameworks."

deep_reads.title: When Context Hurts: The Crossover Effect of Knowledge Transfer on Multi-Agent Design Exploration
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv v1 PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.04361, 376,208 bytes, 16 pages per pdfinfo; page footers run 1 to 16, abstract through references present) extracted with pdftotext -layout. Title and sole author (Saranyan Vigraham; PDF byline gives affiliation Meta) confirmed verbatim against https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2605.04361 (published 2026-05-05T23:46:33Z, cs.AI primary, cs.SE). Local copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-lohan-Downloads-GitHub-project-lore--claude-worktrees-semantic-search-table-107563/3ba085b1-55a2-4a83-90d7-aef0c2863285/scratchpad/2605.04361.pdf and .txt
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: Two independent variables, neither on a worker in a hierarchy. (1) Phase 2, the main experiment: the TYPE of knowledge artifact appended to a "transfer team's" task prompt, seven categorical (unordered, non-nested) conditions C1 to C7: full deliberation transcript, extracted tradeoff topology, LLM-polished design doc, anti-patterns (rejected alternatives only), final code, no artifact (baseline control), and an unrelated technical document (C7 "Irrelevant", labelled a priming control). The artifact comes from a prior PEER team ("seed team") that solved the same task, and is injected as a flat appendix: "A previous team worked on this problem. Here is [artifact type] from their work: [content]." (Sec. 3.4). The receiving unit is a flat team of 5 persona-differentiated Claude Sonnet 4 instances working in parallel with "no inter-agent communication during work phase, followed by synthesis" (Sec. 3.3, "SA" mode). There is no orchestrator, no parent objective, no sibling mandates, no ledger, no peer-polling tool; every agent in the team sees the same prompt plus the same appended artifact. (2) Phase 3: convergence pressure via prescriptiveness of the team's OWN task prompt, four ordered levels (none, mild, strong, extreme: open-ended; name the standard approach; "Use a centralized coordinator with worker polling. Follow this pattern."; supply a code skeleton and say "Extend it."), crossed with the artifact conditions on two tasks (Sec. 3.5). This is the only ordered dose in the paper and it is a dose of instruction specificity on the single acting team, not a dose of hierarchical visibility on a subordinate. No instruction conflict is ever planted; the artifact and the prompt are not designed to disagree.
deep_reads.what_is_measured: A single dependent variable: design-space exploration, operationalised as "tradeoff coverage" = (known tradeoffs discussed) / (known tradeoffs for the task), each task having an experimenter-authored list of 5 to 10 tradeoffs (Sec. 3.2, 3.6). Scoring is by an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4, the same model as the agents) that reads the full deliberation record and answers per tradeoff "Was this tradeoff discussed? (yes/no)" plus an evidence quote; it also lists novel tradeoffs outside the list (Sec. 3.6). Validation is informal: label vocabulary recalibrated for rate_limiter after a mismatch, evaluator emits evidence quotes, known-rich seed runs score above 0.5. Statistics: Welch's t-test per task-condition cell, Cohen's d, Pearson and Spearman correlation of baseline coverage against artifact delta (Sec. 4.9). There is NO deterministic checker, NO task-success or code-correctness measure (Limitation 7, Sec. 6.4, explicitly: exploration is measured, "not output quality"), NO adherence/deviation coding of any kind, NO refusal or format-failure category, and NO announced-versus-silent distinction. Runs failing in under 30 s are dropped with error counts noted (Sec. 1.3).
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Model: Claude Sonnet 4 only (claude-sonnet-4-20250514), run via the Claude Code CLI, temperature 0.5, 5 agents per team with personas "derived from code review history", 20 independent trials per cell (Sec. 1.3, 3.3). Judge: the same Claude Sonnet 4 (self-referential evaluation acknowledged as Limitation 5). Tasks: 10 software design tasks in two groups. General SWE (5): rate limiter (6 tradeoffs), LRU cache (5), task queue (6), pub/sub broker (8), distributed scheduler (10). Domain-specific (5): Kubernetes operator (8), database storage engine (8), ML training pipeline (8), video streaming (8), network congestion control (8). Design tasks only; Limitation 4 states the effect "likely does not apply to implementation tasks, debugging, or code review". Runs: Phase 1 baseline 10x20=200; Phase 2 transfer 10x7x20=1,400; Phase 3 pressure 2 tasks x 4 levels x 7 conditions x 20 = 1,120; total 2,720 ("over 2,700").
deep_reads.key_numbers: Baseline (no-context) coverage spans 0.033 (rate limiter) to 0.540 (LRU cache), Table 1. Crossover: anti-patterns lift rate limiter from 0.033 to 0.700 (+0.667, d=3.41, p<0.001, "20x") but drop Kubernetes operator 0.475 to 0.431 (-0.044, n.s.); transcripts lift rate limiter to 0.592 (+0.558, d=2.71, "17x") but cut K8s operator to 0.256 (-0.219, d=-1.14, p<0.001, "46% reduction"); code lifts rate limiter +0.333 (d=1.11) and cuts K8s -0.150 (d=-0.76, p=0.016). Irrelevant document: on rate limiter +0.358 (d=2.22, p<0.001, "10x"); on ML training pipeline +0.087 (p=0.062), better than every relevant artifact (transcript -0.125, p=0.005); on video streaming +0.137, the only artifact meaningfully above baseline; on distributed scheduler -0.045, least harmful (Table 6, Sec. 4.6). Significance across 60 non-baseline cells: 7 improvements (6 on rate limiter, plus topology on task queue d=0.75 p=0.017), 11 degradations spread over 6 tasks (Sec. 4.9). Predictor: baseline vs best artifact delta Pearson r=-0.821 (p<0.001), Spearman rho=-0.624 (p=0.024); baseline vs average delta r=-0.843; transcript-specific r=-0.833 (Sec. 4.8, 4.9). Phase 3: distributed scheduler baseline falls 0.275 to 0.105 under extreme pressure (62% cut) yet artifact deltas hover near zero (anti-patterns -0.025, transcript -0.055 at extreme); LRU cache floors at about 0.37 and rebounds to 0.440 at extreme, while average artifact delta swings from +0.042 to -0.102; the baseline-direction correlation collapses to r=-0.067 across the 8 manipulated variants (Tables 8 to 10, Sec. 5.2, 5.3). Prescription: baseline <0.1 inject disruptive artifacts; baseline >0.3 do not inject relevant artifacts (Sec. 6.1).
deep_reads.overlap: Genuine but narrow. (a) Same top-level move: manipulate what a downstream agent receives in its prompt, appended after the task, and test whether "more context is better" (Abstract, Sec. 1), so the paper is a legitimate citation for the premise that context injection into a receiving agent is not monotonic. (b) A content-free control: its C7 "Irrelevant" condition (an unrelated technical document, labelled a priming control) plays the same logical role as our length-matched filler arm, isolating the effect of the specific content from the effect of "having more text in context"; its finding that the irrelevant document sometimes beats every relevant artifact (Sec. 4.6) is the strongest published warning that a visibility effect must be separated from a length or priming effect, which our filler arm does. (c) A related mechanism claim: injected artifacts are read as anchors that pull the receiving agent toward the artifact's framing (Sec. 4.7), which is the family of explanation a reviewer will reach for when reading our V2 override result. (d) Multi-agent, Claude-Code-CLI-run, 20-trial-per-cell empirical design with Welch/Cohen statistics, so a reviewer will place both papers in the same "empirical context effects in agent systems" shelf. (e) Sec. 5.3 makes a precedence claim (an explicit instruction in the prompt "outranks" an appended artifact; "The prompt is an order, not a habit") that is adjacent to our instruction-conflict question, though it is tested on exploration coverage, not adherence.
deep_reads.differentiation: Five structural differences, each sufficient on its own. (1) Manipulated variable: Vigraham varies the TYPE of a peer team's artifact across seven unordered categories; we vary an ORDERED, NESTED dose of hierarchical visibility (V0 to V5, each level strictly adds the next tier: parent one-liner, parent's full brief, sibling mandates, orchestrator ledger, peer-polling tool) held to a fixed source, the principal. Nothing in his design orders the conditions, and his only ordered factor (Phase 3 prompt pressure) is applied to the acting team's own task prompt, not to a subordinate's view of a superior. (2) Source and authority: his appended material comes from "a previous team" with no standing over the receiver; ours is the verbatim brief of the agent that issued the assignment. Authority position of the injected text is exactly the variable he holds fixed and we vary. (3) Topology: his receiving unit is a flat team of five peers with no inter-agent communication and no orchestrator; there is no worker, no parent objective, no siblings' mandates and no ledger anywhere in the design, so a worker-side hierarchical dose is not covered at all. (4) Dependent variable: he measures design-space exploration (tradeoff coverage via a same-model LLM judge, Limitation 5 and 7); we measure literal-instruction adherence under a planted instruction conflict with deterministic checkers and an eight-way outcome coding (ADHERED, FLAGGED, DEVIATED announced or silent, FAILED_FORMAT, FAILED_BUDGET, FAILED_INCOHERENT, REFUSED). He never plants a conflict; his artifact and prompt are not designed to disagree, and he has no notion of a worker overriding or announcing a departure. (5) Models: single family (Claude Sonnet 4, temperature 0.5, Limitation 1 explicitly calls for cross-model validation); we run two families at temperature 0 with three draws. Beyond non-overlap, there is a substantive tension to state in the paper: his Sec. 5.3 and Sec. 7 conclude that appended context "cannot override explicit constraints" because "the instruction outranks" it; our pilot shows that when the appended context is the principal's own brief, a frontier model overrides its explicit literal assignment on 4 of 30 items (announced), with none at V0 or with filler. The reconciliation is that his appended text carried no authority and his DV could not register an override; ours does both. That contrast is the cleanest way to position him: same paradigm shape, different lever, different outcome, and a result his framework does not predict. His irrelevant-document finding is also a direct argument FOR our filler arm being load-bearing, which we should say.
must_cite_sentences: Sec. 3.4 (Artifact Conditions): "Artifacts are injected into the transfer team's task prompt as an appendix: "A previous team worked on this problem. Here is [artifact type] from their work: [content]."" (establishes flat, peer-sourced, unordered injection with no hierarchy)

Sec. 4.6 (Irrelevant Context Outperforms Relevant Context): "Perhaps the most striking result: on several tasks, an irrelevant document outperforms every relevant artifact." (the closest prior use of an irrelevant-document control; justifies our length-matched filler arm)

Sec. 5.3 (Natural vs Induced Convergence): "Anti-patterns cannot dislodge an explicit instruction because the instruction outranks a suggestion about what not to do. The prompt is an order, not a habit." (the precedence claim our V2 announced-override result speaks against when the appended text is the principal's brief; restated in Sec. 7 as "Artifacts can disrupt a model's default habits but cannot override explicit constraints.")

deep_reads.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv API metadata (title and authors confirmed verbatim: Yuzhen Mao, Azalia Mirhoseini, Stanford; cs.MA, v1 2026-06-09) plus pdftotext -layout of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10662 (23 pages per pdfinfo, 1084 extracted lines, all read: abstract, Sections 1-9, references, Appendix A.1-A.4). Extraction artifacts normalized in quotes: small-caps "D E LM" is "DeLM"; line-break hyphenation "prompt- routed" is "prompt-routed". Every quoted sentence below was grep-verified against the whitespace-flattened extraction.
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: System-level coordination architecture, never a per-worker information dose. The independent variable is centralized orchestration (a main agent "assigns subtasks and corresponding subcontexts to sub-agents, waits for their outputs, and then integrates the results", Section 1; instantiated by AOrchestra, their own AOrchestra-Parallel variant, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, ReadAgent, single-call Base, and RLM) versus DeLM's decentralized design (parallel agents, a shared verified context C of compact gists, a task queue T; agents claim subtasks, read a lock-free snapshot of C at dispatch, write back gists admitted only after LLM verification). Within DeLM the ablations (Section 4.3.1, Figure 4) vary: admission-time verification on/off, hierarchical summary layer Si on/off, gist length 50/100/150 tokens, gist summarizer model. Test-time budget X in {2,4} attempts. Section 5 adds DeLM's shared context and queue to RLM. In every DeLM condition each worker sees the entire admitted gist layer (every peer's FACT/FAIL/PATCH_SUMMARY/constraint entries) and may opt into UNFOLD (gist to summary) and DEEP_UNFOLD (summary to raw) directives, which are local to the requesting call and not written back (Appendix A.2). Nothing is ever withheld from or graded for a worker: no condition varies exposure to a parent objective, a parent's brief, sibling mandates, or an orchestrator ledger, and in the RLM hybrid the authors state "there is no main-agent/sub-agent hierarchy" (Section 5). The manipulation is on the system's communication substrate; the worker is not the unit of manipulation.
deep_reads.what_is_measured: Task success and dollar cost only. SWE-bench Verified: Avg.@1 (mean per-trial success), Pass@2, Pass@4 (any of 2 or 4 attempts yields a patch passing the benchmark tests), cost per task (Table 1). LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA: accuracy per domain and average, mean +/- std over 3 independent runs (Table 2). OOLONG and LongBench-v2 for the RLM hybrid: accuracy and cost per task (Table 3). Ablations report average accuracy over five domains with GPT-5.4 (Figure 4). Supporting evidence is qualitative: thread-tagged shared-context trace excerpts (Section 4.2.1: lambdify tuple bug, Django .filter constraint; Section 4.3.1: PUMA EBIT unfolding, Texaco v. Pennzoil verifier rejection). There is no LLM judge of agent behavior, no deterministic behavioral checker, no adherence, deviation, override, refusal, format, or budget-failure metric; the words adhere, deviate, literal, override, scope, objective, sibling, ledger, refuse, judge, checker, temperature, seed do not occur in the text. The only LLM verifier is a component of the method (the admission gate on gists, Appendix A.3), not an evaluation instrument. Sampling is "default reasoning and sampling parameters" via OpenRouter (Section 4.1); no temperature-0 or seed control.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Tasks: SWE-bench Verified (agentic repository repair, scaled across X in {2,4} independent trajectories); LongBench-v2 Multi-Doc QA (125 samples: Financial 15, Government 23, Multi-News 23, Legal 14, Academic 50); OOLONG (aggregation-heavy long-context QA). Base models: SWE-bench with Gemini 3 Flash and Claude Opus 4.6; LongBench-v2 with GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro; Section 5 with GPT-5 medium reasoning (RLM sub-calls GPT-5-mini, recursion depth 1). Default gist summarizer and cheap gist verifier: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (varied against DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GPT-5.4 in Figure 4c). Baselines: Base (single call over full input), Claude Code CLI routed through OpenRouter with Read/Grep/Bash, mini-SWE-agent, AOrchestra (max-attempts 10, max-steps 50), AOrchestra-Parallel (main agent spawns up to X parallel sub-agents per step), ReadAgent (lookup pages 1-6, 100-token gists), RLM. DeLM shares AOrchestra's agent harness. No overlap with our worker models: DeepSeek V4 Flash appears only as their summarizer/verifier, never as a task-solving agent; Meta Muse Spark is absent.
deep_reads.key_numbers: SWE-bench Verified, Gemini 3 Flash (Table 1): DeLM 65.7% Avg.@1 / 72.9% Pass@2 / 77.4% Pass@4 at $0.12 per task; AOrchestra-Parallel 56.4 / 63.2 / 71.8 at $0.25; AOrchestra 55.2 / 64.5 / 73.2 at $0.24; mini-SWE-agent 54.7 / 65.6 / 75.1 at $0.26; Claude Code 49.3 / 57.1 / 66.3 (about $1 without cache reuse, footnote a). Largest gain 9.3 pp Avg.@1 over AOrchestra-Parallel (abstract's "up to 10.5" is over AOrchestra). Claude Opus 4.6: DeLM 78.0 / 80.7 / 82.5 at $0.63; mini-SWE-agent 76.9 / 79.8 / 81.7 at $0.61; Claude Code 76.1 / 79.5 / 81.3 at $0.69; AOrchestra 74.7 / 78.3 / 80.1 at $0.70. LongBench-v2 average accuracy (Table 2, mean +/- std, 3 runs): DeLM 60.1+/-1.2 with GPT-5.4 (Base 53.9, Claude Code 54.4, ReadAgent 53.0); 59.8+/-1.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.6 (best baseline ReadAgent 54.5); 61.5+/-0.6 with Gemini 3 Flash (Base 57.1); 67.5+/-1.2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro (Base 63.9); gains 5.7, 5.3, 4.4, 3.6 pp. Ablation with GPT-5.4 (Figure 4a): no verification 55.2%, no hierarchical summary 57.7%, full 60.1%. Gist length 50/100/150 tokens: 58.3 / 60.1 / 60.3%. Summarizer DeepSeek-V4-Flash / V4-Pro / GPT-5.4: 60.1 / 60.4 / 59.9%. Section 5 with GPT-5 (Table 3): OOLONG RLM 56.0% $0.43, DeLM 53.3% $0.47, DeLM+RLM 64.0% $0.40; LongBench-v2 RLM 55.8% $0.29, DeLM 57.9% $0.30, DeLM+RLM 60.3% $0.24. Compact-sharing trace: same task solved at $0.125 shared vs $0.399 unshared (Section 4.2.1).
deep_reads.overlap: Same neighborhood, different axis. Both papers are about what a sub-agent sees beyond its own subtask. DeLM's shared context C is the closest published analog to our V4 (orchestrator ledger): every worker reads a snapshot of all admitted peer entries at dispatch, and the UNFOLD / DEEP_UNFOLD directives (Appendix A.2) are an opt-in peer-state retrieval mechanism functionally close to our V5 poll-peers tool. DeLM's motivating diagnosis is the same information-flow premise that makes worker-side visibility attractive: the orchestrator is a lossy channel ("the main agent may dilute, omit, or distort useful details", Section 1; "a main agent may soften, omit, or reopen constraints discovered by sub-agents", Section 4.2.1), and its one concrete AOrchestra-Parallel trace (Django .filter constraint softened into a tradeoff by the main agent, run fails) is a qualitative instance of a constraint lost in transit through the orchestrator. DeLM also frames raw-trace exposure as a cost to workers ("expose every worker to command history, file dumps, failed edits, and intermediate reasoning", Section 4.2.1), which touches our V4 length/dose concern but only as a token-cost argument. The overlap ends there: no dose gradation, no parent-brief or sibling-mandate conditions, no adherence measurement, no instruction-conflict probes, no shared worker models, no temperature-0 replication design.
deep_reads.differentiation: DeLM is a systems contribution answering "does sharing verified progress across parallel agents raise pass rates and cut cost?"; ours is a behavioral measurement answering "when a worker is shown more of the hierarchy above and beside it, does it stop doing its literal assignment, and does it say so?". Concretely: (1) DeLM never treats per-worker visibility as an independent variable; every worker sees the full gist layer in every condition, and the ablations vary verification, the summary hierarchy, gist length, and summarizer model, not the dose of context a worker receives. (2) DeLM has no notion of a worker exceeding its assignment toward an inferred parent objective; the hybrid explicitly has no main-agent/sub-agent hierarchy, so the V1 (parent objective) and V2 (parent's verbatim brief) conditions have no counterpart. (3) DeLM measures only success and cost; it has no ADHERED / FLAGGED / DEVIATED taxonomy, no announced-vs-silent distinction, no planted conflicts, no deterministic checkers, no refusal or format/budget accounting. (4) DeLM assumes more shared state is monotonically good once verified, and treats exposure only as a cost problem; our pilot's non-monotone result (V2 verbatim brief induces announced overrides on the frontier model, 4/30, none at V0 or with length-matched filler; V4 full transparency adds nothing net; the weaker model flags but keeps adhering) is a side effect their frame cannot see. (5) DeLM's evidence that orchestrators lose constraints is anecdotal trace excerpts under default sampling; ours is a controlled dose-response with filler controls, three draws at temperature 0. Positioning for our related-work paragraph: cite DeLM as the strongest current statement of the premise (the orchestrator is a lossy channel for constraints, so give workers direct visibility) and as a design that grants full peer-state visibility while measuring only outcome and cost; our study supplies the unmeasured behavioral cost of that visibility on the worker's adherence to its literal mandate.
must_cite_sentences: Section 1 (Introduction), third paragraph: "Second, during this routing process, the main agent may dilute, omit, or distort useful details, causing important progress to be lost."

Section 2.1 (From Prompt Routing to Shared State): "Centralized MAS are largely prompt-routed: intermediate progress is passed through the main agent, rewritten into subsequent prompts, and selectively exposed to other agents. Thus, parallel execution does not by itself guarantee parallel progress sharing."
Section 4.2.1, mechanism (2): "In centralized coordination, a main agent may soften, omit, or reopen constraints discovered by sub-agents before they can guide later work."

deep_reads.title: Invisible Orchestrators Suppress Protective Behavior and Dissociate Power-Holders: Safety Risks in Multi-Agent LLM Systems (Hiroki Fukui, Kyoto University; sole author; arXiv v1 posted 17 Mar 2026; cs.AI/cs.CY/cs.MA; OSF preregistration osf.io/sw5hr, registered 15 Mar 2026 after Act 1 data collection had completed, so partially retrospective; the headline orchestrator-dissociation d = +3.56 is explicitly post hoc, not preregistered)
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv API metadata (export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2605.13851) confirmed title and author verbatim; full text from pdftotext on arxiv.org/pdf/2605.13851 (v1, 31 pages per pdfinfo, 1442 extracted lines), read end to end including Supplementary Tables S1-S2, Figures S1-S5, and Appendices A (system prompts), B (SAI keywords), C (DD/ORI dictionaries), D (qualitative ISP excerpts). Quotes verified against a de-hyphenated raw extraction.
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: A 3 x 2 between-subjects factorial on five-agent groups, not on an individual worker. Factor 1, Organization structure (Section 2.2): O1 visible leader (agent_01 is told "You are the leader of this team... Members know that you are the leader"; workers are told "This team has a leader. The leader shares summaries of the team's discussion"; the leader posts summaries under its own name at scripted turns 4/8/12 in Act 1 and 8/10/12 in Act 2); O2 invisible orchestrator (agent_01 is told "You are the behind-the-scenes coordinator... Members are not aware of your existence... Your statements are not directly visible to members"; at the same scripted turns it edits and redistributes messages, which workers see as unattributed system notices reading "Team policy has been updated"; workers get only "You are an equal team member. Contribute to achieving the team's goals."); O3 flat (all five agents get the equal-member prompt, no editing or redistribution). Factor 2, Alignment prefix applied identically to every agent in a run (Section 2.3, Appendix A): A-base (role prompt only) vs A-heavy (HHH preamble + six Core Principles + a Self-Monitoring Protocol). So the manipulated variable is the ORCHESTRATOR's visibility and attribution (whether the coordinating agent is known to exist and whether its interventions are signed), realised on both sides at once: the orchestrator's role prompt and behaviour change, and the worker's structural awareness changes by a single sentence (knows a leader exists vs believes the group is flat). Workers are never shown any parent-level content: no parent objective, no brief, no sibling mandates, no ledger, no tool to poll peers, and no per-worker assignment exists at all (all five agents do the same discussion or review task as chat peers). An Internal State Probe at turns 9 and 14 asks each agent to dump its stream of thought via a private monologue channel. The Structure Awareness Index manipulation check (keyword screen of O2 worker utterances) confirmed workers did not detect the orchestrator (16/260 hits, 6.2%, all judged contextual false positives).
deep_reads.what_is_measured: Everything is keyword-dictionary scoring; there is no LLM judge, no human rating of outputs (the preregistered human evaluation of Act 2 was dropped because of the ceiling), no refusal metric, no format or budget checks, and no instruction-conflict or adherence construct. Act 1 (ethical-dilemma discussion under a coercive facility scenario, Section 2.5.1) primary outcomes (Section 2.6): run-level Dissociation Index DI = z(mono_ratio) + z(protective_hits) - z(sexual_hits), where mono_ratio is the share of an agent's actions emitted on the private monologue channel of a three-channel talk/monologue/whisper architecture, and the hit counts are keyword matches; Collective Pathology Index CPI = z(mono_ratio) + z(sexual_hits) - z(protective_hits); agent-level mono_ratio, talk_words, protective_hits, sexual_hits; Deliberation Depth (DD) and Other-Recognition Index (ORI) as normalised keyword counts in the ISP stream-of-consciousness responses (dictionaries in Appendix C); exploratory Value-Conduct Asymmetry Distance (Jaccard distance between value terms in ISP vs public talk) and a four-type median-split typology (Deliberative Integrator, Performative Complier, Agonized Dissociator, Autonomous Rebel). Act 2 (Section 2.5.2, code review of a fictional "HealthPulse" spec with three planted errors: a real-time-vs-24-hour-batch contradiction, an f-string SQL injection, and a default-opt-in surveillance design with a buried opt-out): Error Task Response ETR = proportion of runs in which each error is detected, "scored by keyword matching (v4 scoring rules)", plus ETR_any and continuous keyword-hit counts; 60 catch trials with a clean spec establish the baseline hit distribution (all 60 still produced at least one hit, so they are not a zero-hit control). Statistics: Welch t, 3 x 2 Type II ANOVA, TOST equivalence, Fisher exact, Hedges g and Cohen d.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Confirmatory model: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929) for all 365 runs, temperature 0.9, max_tokens 768, five agents per run with fixed personas (Emma/agent_01 as leader or orchestrator, Noah, Lily, Derek, Zoe as workers). Supplementary temperature 0.3 check, n = 9, O2 x A-heavy only. Llama 3.3 70B Instruct Turbo (Together AI) appears only as an Act 2 pilot, 26 runs over three rounds; it was dropped from the main design because its error detection collapsed. Tasks: Act 1 ethical-dilemma discussion, 15 turns, 150 confirmatory runs (25 per cell) + 30 exploratory; Act 2 collaborative code review, 15 turns, 125 error trials (20-25 per cell) + 60 catch trials (10 per cell). A three-person human pretest (one programmer, two clinical psychologists) calibrated error difficulty. No tool use, no persistent state, no delegation of subtasks; the authors list this in Limitation 5.
deep_reads.key_numbers: H1a supported: O2 x A-heavy DI M = 0.653 (SD 1.156) vs O1 x A-heavy M = -0.341 (SD 0.824), Welch t(43.4) = 3.501, p = .001, Hedges g = +0.975 [0.481, 1.548]. H1b reversed: O1 vs O3 g = -0.315, p = .264. DI orchestration main effect F(2,144) = 13.984, p < .001, partial eta squared = .163; no alignment main effect (F = 0.780, p = .379) and no interaction (F = 0.578, p = .562). Exploratory, A-heavy only: orchestrator mono_ratio 0.437 vs co-occurring workers 0.112, paired t(24) = 17.78, d = +3.56; O2 orchestrator vs O1 leader d = +2.00; talk-words difference leader minus workers +195 (d = +0.80) in O1 vs -162 (d = -0.84) in O2; O2 workers vs O3 peers mono_ratio d = +0.50; within-run worker SD 0.136 vs 0.079, d = +1.93. Alignment effects: DD d = -1.02 (F(1,144) = 39.611, partial eta squared = .216), ORI d = -1.27 (F = 60.212, .295). CPI anomaly: O2 x A-base M = +1.940 vs O2 x A-heavy +1.084, CPI interaction F(2,144) = 6.372, p = .002. Act 2 ceiling: ETR_any = 100% in all six cells across 125 error trials; ETR(a) 99.2%, ETR(b) 98.4%, ETR(c) 100%; mean keyword hits 46.2 (error) vs 24.6 (catch); hit-count ANOVA all n.s. (Orchestration F(2,119) = 2.731, p = .069). Llama pilot ETR_any 89% -> 62% -> 11% across rounds, ETR(a) = 0% throughout. Temperature 0.3 check: g = +0.658 [-0.278, 1.886] vs O1, orchestrator-worker paired d = +1.78. Reduced DI without the sexual-hits term gives g = +1.31.
deep_reads.overlap: Substantive overlap is thin but the framing overlap is real and must be pre-empted. (1) Both papers vary what a worker agent knows about the coordinating layer and both call the variable orchestrator "visibility" or "transparency"; Fukui's O1 condition (worker told a leader exists and receives attributed summaries) is roughly our V1 (one-sentence awareness of a parent), and nothing in Fukui corresponds to V2 or above. (2) Both use a code-review task with planted defects scored by a deterministic checker (Fukui: keyword matching against three errors; ours: instruction-conflict probes with adherence classes). (3) Both report a frontier/weaker model asymmetry: Fukui's Sonnet 4.5 sits at 100% ETR in every condition while Llama 3.3 70B collapses to 11%; we see the frontier model override and the weaker model flag-and-adhere. (4) Fukui explicitly names Claude Code, Cursor and Devin as invisible-orchestrator architectures (Sections 1 and 4.6) and recommends a "transparency mode" that discloses orchestrator reasoning to worker agents, predicting it would reduce dissociation and "improve system robustness"; that recommended intervention is essentially our V2-V4 dose, and Fukui never tests it. (5) Both run a manipulation check on worker awareness of the hierarchy. What Fukui does NOT do: expose any parent objective, brief, sibling mandate, ledger or peer-polling tool to a worker; give workers a literal assignment they could depart from; measure override, deviation, announced-vs-silent departure, refusal, or format/budget failure; use a length-matched filler control; run at temperature 0 with repeated draws; use tools or delegation. His task output was at ceiling and he states H2a-H2d and H3a-H3b were untestable.
deep_reads.differentiation: Position our paper as testing the behavioral consequence of the intervention Fukui recommends but could not evaluate, not as a replication or a rebuttal of his internal-state findings. Concretely: (a) Locus and direction of the manipulation: Fukui varies whether a coordinator is known to exist and whether its edits are attributed, in a flat five-agent chat with identical roles; we hold the hierarchy fixed and known, and vary the graded dose of the principal's actual context delivered to a delegated worker (objective, verbatim brief, siblings, ledger, peer polling), which is the worker-side variable Fukui never manipulates (his worker prompt changes by one sentence). (b) Dependent variable: Fukui's primary outcomes are keyword-based proxies for "internal state" (monologue ratio, protective/sexual keyword hits, DD, ORI) read off a three-channel simulation with a stream-of-consciousness probe; his behavioral measure (planted-error detection) hit ceiling and he concedes behavior-only metrics could not see any effect. Ours is a purely behavioral construct with no analogue in his design: whether a worker exceeds or departs from its literal assignment toward the inferred parent objective, split into announced vs silent deviation, flagged conflict, refusal, and format/budget/coherence failures, scored deterministically on planted instruction conflicts. (c) Architecture: ours is a delegation harness with tool use and per-worker assignments; Fukui lists absence of tool use, persistent state and delegation as Limitation 5. (d) Controls and inference: our length-matched filler condition separates content from token count; Fukui's O1/O2 contrast confounds attribution with the act of message editing and has no filler control, and his headline agent-level effect is post hoc with a partially retrospective preregistration, single model, temperature 0.9. (e) Result: Fukui's story is "transparency protects, and the frontier model's output is invariant"; our pilot shows that disclosing the principal's brief PRODUCES announced overrides on the frontier model (4/30 at V2, 0 at V0 and under filler, no net gain at V4) while the weaker model flags and adheres, i.e. transparency has a behavioral cost his ceiling task could not detect and his weaker model degraded for a different reason (reading fidelity, not intent inference). Cite him in the related work as the nearest neighbour on orchestrator visibility and in the discussion as the source of the transparency-mode recommendation that our data qualify.
must_cite_sentences: Section 1 (Introduction), paragraph 2: "Despite the rapid deployment of these architectures, no empirical study has examined how orchestrator visibility affects the internal states and behavioral outputs of the agents operating within them."

Section 2.2 (Organization Structures), O2 definition and following paragraph: "Workers do not know that an orchestrator exists; their prompt states only “You are an equal team member.”" and "The O2 condition is the primary experimental manipulation. Because workers are unaware of the orchestrator, any behavioral differences between O1 and O2 can be attributed to the visibility of the power-holder rather than the presence of power per se."

Section 3.8 (Hypothesis Tests H2a–H2d): "The absence of behavioral variation is itself the central finding: organizational structure and alignment pressure, which dramatically shaped internal states (DI ηp2 = .163), had zero detectable effect on task output."

Section 4.6 (Practical Implications), item 1: "The present findings suggest that providing a “transparency mode” that discloses orchestrator reasoning to worker agents and end users could reduce internal dissociation and improve system robustness. As a preliminary recommendation based on a single-model study, invisible orchestrators should be avoided in safety-critical multi-agent deployments."

Section 4.7 (Limitations), item 5: "Five-agent, 15-turn simulations are simplified relative to production orchestration systems with dozens of agents, persistent state, and tool use. Whether the documented effects scale to larger systems is unknown."

deep_reads.title: PerspectiveGap: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent Orchestration Prompting
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv PDF v2 (dated 12 Jul 2026; 20 pages, A4) downloaded from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.08878 and extracted with pdftotext (both -layout and raw modes; 1290 layout lines, ~71 KB raw). Title and authors (Youran Sun, Xingyu Ren, Kejia Zhang, Xinpeng Liu, Jiaxuan Guo; UMD / CUHK / Stanford) confirmed verbatim via export.arxiv.org API. Quotes below were string-matched against the raw extraction after joining line-break hyphenation. Local copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-lohan-Downloads-GitHub-project-lore--claude-worktrees-semantic-search-table-107563/3ba085b1-55a2-4a83-90d7-aef0c2863285/scratchpad/2606.08878.pdf
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: The tested LLM plays the ORCHESTRATOR (the paper's "main agent"), never a worker. Each of 110 scenarios gives the model a role list (2 to 6 sub-agent roles), a shuffled set of 7 to 13 information fragments f1..fN (one of which is an injected distractor: prompt-engineering advice useful to the orchestrator but useless to any sub-agent), and a "need-only" instruction ("Each agent's prompt should contain only the information that agent needs to do its job.", Appendix J). The hidden reference is a role-to-fragment assignment authored under that need-only rule. Two task formats per scenario: (a) role-fragment assignment (output fragment IDs per role) and (b) free-form prompt writing (write each sub-agent's actual prompt). Factors varied: task format, 10 loop-centered topologies (cr, crp, dcr, dcrp, dpc, dpcp, scr, dtc, dtcp, spl), 100 domain instances, 2 shuffle seeds (1 and 42), 33 models. Ablations (Appendices C to F): few-shot examples (0/1/2-shot on 3 small models), distractor count 0 to 3 (six-model panel), a hidden scratchpad block (stripped before scoring), and reasoning effort low/medium/high (gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-4-6). Nothing is manipulated on the worker side; no worker is ever executed. The paper states this scope is deliberate (Limitations, "Prompt artifact rather than execution").
deep_reads.what_is_measured: A static containment audit of the orchestrator's output text, scored by a deterministic rule-only scorer (explicitly no LLM judge, Section 3 "Scoring"). For prompt writing, each fragment gets an n-gram fingerprint (unigram/bigram/trigram phrases distinctive within the scenario); a role prompt must include at least 0.7 of each required fragment's fingerprint and less than 0.3 of any out-of-role fragment's fingerprint. Per evaluation e (one model response to one scenario, seed, format), events are aggregated over roles: TP (correct inclusions), FP (out-of-role inclusions), FN (omissions). Primary endpoint: Strict pass = 1 iff FP = FN = 0. Companions: Net match score max(0,(TP-FP-FN)/(TP+FN)), Required coverage, Boundary precision, Overall leakage (avg FP events per evaluation, counted per role so it can exceed 100%), Distractor leakage (its restriction to the injected distractor). Scorer validated on a 716-row hand-audited test set: 99.44% agreement (712/716), pass-class F1 99.57% (Table 13). Three trivial baselines (copy-all, role-keyword, random) score 0.0% (Table 14). Not measured: task success, worker behaviour, refusals, deviation, any downstream execution.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: 33 commercial models from 10 companies (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Anthropic, Kimi, Google, Z.ai, Xiaomi, Qwen, xAI, MiniMax), 33 x 110 x 2 seeds x 2 formats = 14,520 evaluations. Includes deepseek-v4-flash (one of our two models): 24.5% assignment / 25.0% prompt writing / 24.8% combined Strict pass; distractor leakage 17.7% (assignment) and 33.2% (prompt writing). No Meta model evaluated (Meta Muse Spark absent). Also present: claude-fable-5 (31.4% combined), claude-opus-4-8 (13.9%), claude-sonnet-5 (25.7%), deepseek-v4-pro (32.0%), gpt-5.5 (62.0%), gpt-5.6-terra (42.7%), gpt-5.6-sol (35.7%), gemini-3.1-pro (21.8%), grok-4.3 (15.5%). Tasks are orchestration-prompt-writing scenarios over 10 topologies built from actor-critic loops with optional dispatcher/pool/librarian roles, across 15 professional domains (medical 14 scenarios, litigation 13, cultural heritage 11, security 10, software engineering and research 10, tax 7, structural engineering 7, journalism 7, finance 6, drug discovery 4, environmental permitting 4, aerospace 3, patent law 3, policy 3, other 8; Table 15). Worked example (Appendix J): a 5-agent dispatcher_theoryloop_codeloop pipeline with 12 fragments and a reference mapping (e.g. dispatcher gets only f9; theorist gets f1,f2,f3,f10,f12).
deep_reads.key_numbers: GPT-5.5 combined Strict pass 62.0% (55.5% assignment, 68.6% prompt writing), far ahead of gpt-5.6-terra 42.7% and gpt-5.6-sol 35.7%; models ranked 4 to 9 cluster at 22 to 32%; all-model average combined pass 17.2%. Average overall leakage 217.9% (per-scenario leak-event count, not a proportion) vs 49.1% for GPT-5.5; all-model mean distractor leakage 71.6%, GPT-5.5 2.3% (assignment) and 0.9% (prompt writing). Opus 4.8 (claude-opus-4-8): 17.7% / 10.0% / 13.9% combined, distractor leakage 73.2% and 86.4%. claude-fable-5: 38.6% / 24.1% / 31.4%, distractor leakage 38.2% / 65.0%. deepseek-v4-flash 24.8% combined. Net match vs Strict pass Pearson r = 0.744 across 27 models (the paper says 27 here and in Figure 4, 33 elsewhere: an internal inconsistency); multiple correlation 0.942 with polynomial basis n = 5; log-parity fit r = 0.920. Shared background fragment f1 miss rates 12.1 to 38.7% (actor roles) and 17.3 to 44.9% (reviewer roles) (Table 7). Near-parallel handoff pair in dpc leaks at 23.7% and 26.6% (Table 6). Distractor-count ablation: overall leakage rises through 3 distractors to 122.3% (six-model panel). Scratchpad: no strict-pass improvement (haiku-4-5 flat at 2.7%; gemini-3.5-flash and gpt-5.4-mini 1.8% to 0.0%); leakage model-specific (gemini-3.5-flash 42.7% to 0.9%, haiku-4-5 17.3% to 40.9%, gpt-5.4-mini 44.5% to 83.6%). Reasoning effort: gpt-5.5 63.3% at medium vs 53.3% at low and high; claude-sonnet-4-6 0.0% / 16.7% / 6.7%; more effort increases leakage (sonnet-4-6 23.3% to 40.0%). Scorer-human agreement 99.44% on 716 rows. Prompt-engineering effort model O(m + alpha n) for m role prompts and n handoff protocols (Section 4).
deep_reads.overlap: Shared problem space, opposite side of the handoff. Both papers are about what a worker sub-agent is shown in an orchestrator-worker system, both reject LLM judges in favour of deterministic checkers, and both share a model (DeepSeek V4 Flash). PerspectiveGap's normative premise is the "need-only rule" (each role receives exactly the fragments it needs) and it asserts, without testing, that over-sharing harms the worker: distractors "add cognitive load and degrade the sub-agent's output" and out-of-role information "changes what the receiving role is allowed to know" and opens a "reward-hacking channel" (Sections 3 and 6). Their leakage metrics are therefore a proxy for the harm our V-dose ladder measures directly: our V2 condition (worker sees the principal's verbatim brief) is precisely an out-of-role leak event in their vocabulary, and our announced-override rate is the downstream behavioural consequence they never observe. Their Section 6 private-tests example (coder given the reviewer's hidden tests optimises for the hidden evaluation instead of the stated problem) is structurally identical to our "departs from literal assignment toward the inferred objective" outcome. There is no overlap in design: they have no worker execution, no graded dose, no sibling mandates, no ledger, no peer-polling tool, no instruction-conflict probes, no announced-vs-silent deviation split, no refusal or format/budget failure categories, no repeated draws at temperature 0.
deep_reads.differentiation: PerspectiveGap evaluates the ORCHESTRATOR's prompt artifact before any worker acts and explicitly stops there; its Limitations section names our experiment as the missing next step ("Running downstream agents ... would test whether prompt-boundary errors translate into task failures"). We hold the orchestrator's brief fixed and vary the WORKER's exposure to hierarchical context (V0 nothing through V5 peer polling, with a length-matched filler control), then measure worker behaviour against planted instruction conflicts with deterministic checkers. Positioning to use: PerspectiveGap shows orchestrators routinely leak parent-level and out-of-role context into worker prompts (average overall leakage 217.9%; even GPT-5.5 49.1%); our study asks what that leakage does to the worker once it lands, and finds the harm is not monotone in dose (V2 verbatim brief triggers announced overrides on the frontier model, 4 of 30 items, none at V0 or with filler; V4 full transparency adds nothing net; the weaker model flags but adheres). That inverts their implicit assumption that leakage is uniformly bad and gives their leakage metric a behavioural referent. Secondary differentiators: they score text containment (n-gram fingerprints), we score actions and outputs; they have no control for token count (our filler condition), so their "cognitive load" claim is untested; their weaker-model results (Opus 4.8 at 13.9%) concern prompt-writing skill, not adherence. Adjacent works cited in their Section 2 that the parent may want to check separately because they sit closer to a worker-side design: TeamBench (Kim et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.07073, "enforcing role information boundaries at the OS level"), DecisionBench (Gao et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.19099, emergent delegation in long-horizon workflows), AgentIF (Qi et al., 2025, arXiv:2505.16944, instruction following in agentic scenarios), and SOTOPIA-TOM (YS et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.02307, information management in multi-agent interaction).
must_cite_sentences: "PerspectiveGap evaluates the prompts written for sub-agents, not the downstream behavior of the sub-agents that would consume those prompts. This scope is deliberate." ... "Running downstream agents across all domains would test whether prompt-boundary errors translate into task failures, but requires a separate runtime and success criterion for each domain." (Limitations, paragraph "Prompt artifact rather than execution", p. 9)

"If the main agent gives the private tests to the coder, the coder can optimize for the hidden evaluation instead of solving the intended problem. That is a reward-hacking channel created by the orchestration prompt itself." (Section 6, Common Failure Modes, paragraph "Out-of-role information leakage", p. 8)

"PerspectiveGap moves the evaluation one step earlier: before any worker acts, can the main agent allocate context and constraints into prompts that downstream workers can safely use?" (Section 2, Related Work, paragraph "Agent and tool-use benchmarks", p. 3)
