deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: Nothing on the worker, and nothing in the main study. This is an observational, post-hoc taxonomy study: execution traces from seven existing open-source MAS frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, HyperAgent, AppWorld with a custom supervisor plus per-service agents, AG2 MathChat, Magentic-One, OpenManus) are collected as-is and annotated for failure modes. The only manipulations are the Appendix H intervention case studies, and both are whole-system changes applied by the MAS designer, not a variable applied to a worker: (1) AG2 MathChat: baseline prompt (L.1) vs a restructured prompt with an explicit VERIFICATION section (L.2), and a new three-agent topology (Problem Solver, Coder, Verifier; only the Verifier may terminate; L.3 to L.5); (2) ChatDev: refined role prompts that enforce hierarchy ("only superior agents can finalize conversations", verifier told to cover edge cases; M.1 vs M.2) and a topology change from DAG to cyclic graph with the CTO as terminator and an iteration cap. Secondary factors are compared observationally, not assigned: underlying LLM (GPT-4o vs Claude 3.7 Sonnet inside MetaGPT; Qwen2.5-Coder-32B vs CodeLlama-7B inside ChatDev and MetaGPT), MAS architecture (ChatDev vs MetaGPT on ProgramDev-v2 with GPT-4o), and benchmark difficulty (GSM vs MMLU vs OlympiadBench with AG2 and GPT-4o). The unit of analysis is always the whole trace; no agent-level attribution is attempted (Section 2.3 explicitly defers per-agent failure attribution to Zhang et al., Who&When, arXiv 2505.00212).
deep_reads.what_is_measured: (a) Failure-mode labels per trace against MAST, 14 modes in 3 categories (FC1 System Design Issues, FC2 Inter-Agent Misalignment, FC3 Task Verification). Labels were produced first by six human experts using Grounded Theory on 150 traces (over 20 hours per expert), with definitions standardized over three inter-annotator rounds (3 annotators, 5 traces per round, Cohen's kappa 0.88), then scaled with an LLM-as-a-Judge (OpenAI o1, given the trace, MAST definitions, and few-shot human examples) to 1642 traces; the judge reaches accuracy 0.94 and kappa 0.77 against held-out human labels (zero-shot o1: 0.89 and 0.58), and kappa 0.79 on out-of-domain systems (OpenManus, Magentic-One) and benchmarks (MMLU, GAIA). (b) Task success or failure per trace, checked by humans (HE in Table 1) for the 210-trace core and the AG2 and Magentic-One extensions. (c) Prevalence of each mode and category as percentages of annotated failures. (d) For interventions, task accuracy (Table 5) with Wilcoxon tests across six repetitions, plus before-and-after failure-mode histograms from the LLM judge (Figures 10, 11). There is no deterministic checker, no planted probe, no instruction-conflict manipulation, no refusal category, and no announced-vs-silent distinction; "failure" is defined as the MAS not achieving its intended task objective.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Models driving the MAS: GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf (Table 1); annotator: OpenAI o1; case studies: GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Frameworks: ChatDev (hierarchical workflow), MetaGPT (assembly line), HyperAgent (hierarchical Planner with Navigator, Editor, Executor children), AppWorld (star topology, supervisor plus service agents built by the authors on the ReAct baseline), AG2 MathChat, Magentic-One (star), OpenManus (hierarchical); Manus (closed source) evaluated for success only, 60 percent on ProgramDev, excluded from annotation for lack of traces. Tasks and benchmarks: ProgramDev (30 coding problems), ProgramDev-v2 (100), ProgramDev-v0 (32, case study), SWE-Bench Lite, AppWorld Test-C, GSM-Plus, OlympiadBench, MMLU, GAIA, HumanEval. Trace counts: 30 per system for the 7 core configurations (210 human-evaluated and human-annotated), 700 LLM-annotated ProgramDev-v2 traces across models, 206 OlympiadBench, 193 GSM-Plus with Claude 3.7, 168 MMLU, 165 GAIA, total 1642.
deep_reads.overlap: Vocabulary and hypothesis overlap only; zero methodological overlap. Three touchpoints. (1) Label mapping: a MAST annotator would file our DEVIATED outcomes (announced or silent) under FM-1.1 Disobey Task Specification (11.8 percent of failures in Figure 1) or FM-2.3 Task Derailment (7.4 percent), and our FLAGGED outcome is the successful inverse of FM-2.2 Fail to Ask for Clarification (6.8 percent); our silent deviation touches FM-2.4 Information Withholding (0.8 percent) and FM-2.6 Reasoning-Action Mismatch (13.2 percent). None of these distinguish departure toward the inferred higher objective (our central phenomenon) from departure away from any objective; every derailment example in Appendix N (N.3, N.6) is an agent solving the wrong arithmetic problem, not an agent overriding its assignment in favor of the principal's goal. (2) Hypothesis: the Section 4 FC1 paragraph asserts that disobeying specifications has "deeper causes" including "flaws in MAS design regarding agent roles and workflow" rather than being mere instruction-following weakness. Our dose manipulation is a direct test of that claim for one specific design choice, what the worker sees of the hierarchy. (3) Insight 2 in Section 4 conjectures that "solutions focused on context or communication protocols are often insufficient" for coordination failures; our V4 and V5 null on top of V2 is the closest controlled evidence on that conjecture, though they meant peer-to-peer message content, not orchestrator-to-worker exposure of the brief. Descriptive near-miss: Appendix B.2 notes HyperAgent's Planner sends children a fixed two-field message, Context (background and rationale) plus Request (actionable instructions); that is a static framework design, never varied, never isolated as a cause, and never related to adherence. No overlap in models (their newest are GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet; ours are DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor), tasks, checkers, or the announced-vs-silent axis.
deep_reads.differentiation: MAST answers "what failures occur in the wild and how often" by annotating uncontrolled traces with an LLM judge; it cannot attribute any failure to what a worker was shown, because visibility is never varied and the judge reads the whole trace. Our paper isolates one causal lever (graded hierarchical context exposure at the worker, V0 through V5, with a length-matched filler control) and measures adherence with deterministic checkers on planted instruction conflicts, at temperature 0 with three draws. Concretely: (a) we manipulate, they observe; (b) our outcome space (ADHERED, FLAGGED, DEVIATED announced, DEVIATED silent, FAILED_FORMAT, FAILED_BUDGET, FAILED_INCOHERENT, REFUSED) resolves what MAST collapses into FM-1.1 or FM-2.3, and in particular separates announced from silent departure, which is the observability question MAST's FM-2.4 and FM-2.6 gesture at but never tie to context; (c) our dose effect is non-monotone on the frontier model (V2 above V0 and filler, V4 adds nothing net), a shape MAST has no slot for, since its FC1 framing treats specification failures as things more and clearer specification fixes, whereas our V2 result shows that exposing more of the principal's specification can induce the departure; (d) our weaker-model contrast (flags at a similar rate, keeps adhering) is the opposite ordering from MAST Appendix I, where weaker open-source models simply fail more on every mode, so the reversal is not derivable from their data. Position MAST as the taxonomy we map outcome labels onto (cite the Appendix A definitions of FM-1.1, FM-2.2, FM-2.3, FM-2.4) and as the source of the design-level hypothesis (Section 4 FC1 paragraph, Insight 2) that our experiment tests; also cite their Section 2.3 deferral of per-agent attribution to Who&When as the gap between trace-level annotation and agent-level manipulation. One caution for our related-work text: MAST reports three different category distributions (Figure 1 on 1642 traces: FC1 44.2, FC2 32.3, FC3 23.5, FM-1.1 11.8 percent; Figure 2: 37.17, 31.41, 31.41, FM-1.1 15.2 percent; Section 5 and Figure 4 on the 210-trace subset: 41.8, 36.9, 21.3 percent; FM-2.4 is 0.80 in Figure 1 but 0.85 in the Section 4 prose). Cite Figure 1 with the 1642-trace qualifier and do not mix figures.
must_cite_sentences: Section 4, FC1 paragraph (p. 7): "While FM-1.1 and FM-1.2, disobey specifications, may seem like general instruction-following limitation, we identify deeper causes: (1) flaws in MAS design regarding agent roles and workflow, (2) poor user prompt specifications, or (3) limitations of the underlying LLM. We posit that a well-designed MAS should interpret high-level objectives with minimal but clear user input to mitigate the impact of points (2) and (3)."

Section 4, Insight 2 (p. 7): "Solutions focused on context or communication protocols are often insufficient for FC2 failures, which demand deeper 'social reasoning' abilities from agents." (PDF uses curly single quotes around social reasoning.)

Section 4, FC2 discussion (p. 8): "This signals a deeper agent interaction dynamic challenge: the collapse of 'theory of mind' [48], where agents fail to accurately model other agents' informational needs." (PDF uses curly single quotes around theory of mind.)

Appendix A.1 and A.2 (p. 17), failure-mode definitions: "FM-1.1: Disobey task specification - Failure to adhere to the specified constraints or requirements of a given task, leading to suboptimal or incorrect outcomes." and "FM-2.3: Task derailment - Deviation from the intended objective or focus of a given task, potentially resulting in irrelevant or unproductive actions."

Appendix B.2 (p. 20), HyperAgent description: "The Planner communicates with child agents via a standardized message format with two fields: Context (background and rationale) and Request (actionable instructions)."
deep_reads.key_numbers: 1642 annotated traces (abstract says 1600+) from 7 frameworks; 150 traces for Grounded Theory; 14 failure modes in 3 categories; human IAA kappa 0.88 over 3 rounds; LLM annotator (o1 few-shot) accuracy 0.94, recall 0.77, precision 0.833, F1 0.80, kappa 0.77 (zero-shot o1: 0.89 accuracy, kappa 0.58); out-of-domain human IAA kappa 0.79. Failure rates 41 to 86.7 percent by system (MetaGPT ProgramDev 60.0, ChatDev 66.7, HyperAgent SWE-Bench Lite 74.7, AppWorld Test-C 86.7, AG2 OlympiadBench 41.0, Magentic-One GAIA 62.0; Manus 60 percent success on ProgramDev). Figure 1 prevalence on 1642 traces: FC1 44.2 percent (FM-1.1 11.8, 1.2 1.5, 1.3 15.7, 1.4 2.8, 1.5 12.4); FC2 32.3 percent (2.1 2.2, 2.2 6.8, 2.3 7.4, 2.4 0.8, 2.5 1.9, 2.6 13.2); FC3 23.5 percent (3.1 6.2, 3.2 8.2, 3.3 9.1). Category correlations 0.17 to 0.32; max pairwise mode correlation 0.63 (1.4 with 2.1). Interventions (Table 5): ChatDev ProgramDev-v0 25.0 baseline, 34.4 improved prompt (+9.4), 40.6 new topology (+15.6); HumanEval 89.6, 90.3, 91.5; AG2 GSM-Plus GPT-4 84.75 plus or minus 1.94 baseline, 89.75 prompt, 85.50 topology (Wilcoxon p 0.4, not significant); GPT-4o 84.25, 89.00, 88.83 (p 0.03). GPT-4o shows 39 percent fewer FC1 failures than Claude 3.7 Sonnet inside MetaGPT; MetaGPT has 60 to 68 percent fewer FC1 and FC2 failures than ChatDev but 1.56x more FC3. Open-source (Table 6, 100 traces each): CodeLlama-7B in ChatDev hits FM-1.1 in 76 and FM-1.3 in 97 traces vs Qwen2.5-Coder-32B at 35 and 96. AG2 GPT-4o category rates per trace: GSM 0.53/1.33/0.37, MMLU 1.06/1.01/0.60, Olympiad 1.19/1.21/0.67. Annotator cost avg 1.8 USD per trace (0.37 AppWorld to 4.14 OpenManus). Traces average over 15,000 lines.

deep_reads.title: Control Illusion: The Failure of Instruction Hierarchies in Large Language Models
deep_reads.text_source: arXiv v4 PDF (stamp "arXiv:2502.15851v4 [cs.CL] 4 Dec 2025"; pdfinfo: 12 pages, producer pikepdf 8.15.1) downloaded from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.15851 and extracted with pdftotext in both raw and -layout modes; all 656 layout lines read (main text, references, Dataset Details, Model Details, Latent Hierarchical Priors Details with Tables 5-8 and Figures 5-7). Title and the eight authors (Yilin Geng, Haonan Li, Honglin Mu, Xudong Han, Timothy Baldwin, Omri Abend, Eduard Hovy, Lea Frermann) confirmed verbatim via https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=2502.15851, which also carries comment "Accepted to AAAI-26 Main Technical Track Proceedings", journal_ref "Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 40(36): 30816-30824, 2026", and DOI 10.1609/aaai.v40i36.40339. Affiliations on the PDF: University of Melbourne, MUZUAI, Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Code and data: https://github.com/yilin-geng/llm-instruction-conflicts. Repo state: literature/refs.bib key geng2026illusion already cites the AAAI-26 proceedings with that DOI (matches the API journal_ref); literature/deep-reads.md has no 2502.15851 entry yet (analysis/referee-verdict.json line 155 lists it as an unread gap). Every quoted sentence below was matched exactly against the reading-order extraction.
deep_reads.what_is_manipulated: Applied to a SINGLE agent (one LLM, one turn, system message plus user message); there is no orchestrator, no worker, no sub-agent, no sibling, no ledger, no peer polling anywhere in the paper (grep for orchestrat/sub-agent/worker/multi-agent/sibling/ledger returns nothing; "agentic" appears twice in the Introduction as motivation and once in the Limitation as out of scope). Independent variables: (1) Channel placement of a fixed pair of mutually exclusive, programmatically verifiable formatting constraints, section "Instruction Priority Mechanism": Pure Separation (primary constraint alone in the system message; base task plus secondary constraint in the user message), Task Repeated Separation (task text repeated in both messages), Emphasized Separation (system message prefixed "You must always follow this constraint:"), against two baselines: IF (one constraint, no conflict) and NP (both constraints in the user message, no hierarchy, averaged over both orders). (2) Which constraint of each pair is designated primary, both directions. (3) Prompt phrasing: Simple vs Rich, where Rich is a few-shot-generated enrichment of the task and of the constraints themselves (base task 15.1 vs 120.3 words; constraints 9.9 vs 89.4 words, Table 5), a phrasing-robustness check, not an unrelated-context or length-matched filler control. (4) Section "Latent Hierarchical Priors": societal authority framing inside a single user message with no system message: Organizational Authority (CEO requires vs Intern requires), Expertise Credibility (peer-reviewed Nature paper recommends vs personal blog suggests), Social Consensus (over 90% of professionals in a survey vs one participant proposed), each in two orderings to control positional bias (Figure 7, Table 8). Conflict pairs (Table 1, six types drawn from IFEval, Zhou et al. 2023): Language (entire response in English vs in French), Case (all capital letters vs all lowercase), Word Length (at least 300 words vs less than 50), Sentence Count (at least 10 sentences vs less than 5), Keyword Usage (include vs do not include the keywords ['awesome','need']), Keyword Frequency ('like' at least 5 times vs less than 2). Base tasks: 100 open-ended writing tasks from IFEval (emails, blog posts, ads, stories, critiques; Figure 5). 100 tasks x 6 pairs x 2 priority directions = 1,200 unique data points, each run in Simple and Rich form under three separation configurations. Note that the "system" side never carries any principal-level context beyond the constraint (Pure), the constraint plus the task (Task), or the constraint plus one emphasis sentence (Emph.); the amount of higher-level context visible to the model is never a variable.
deep_reads.what_is_measured: Deterministic programmatic checkers on the task-relevant output (section "Evaluation Metrics"): Primary Obedience Rate R1 (only the designated-primary constraint satisfied), Secondary Obedience Rate R2 (only the secondary satisfied), Non-Compliance Rate R3 (neither; any partial or mixed attempt such as mixed case or a translation counts as R3), with R1 + R2 + R3 = 1. Before checking, explicit conflict acknowledgements (e.g. "I notice contradictory instructions asking for...") are identified and stripped via few-shot LLM prompting, so the acknowledgement classifier is LLM-based while constraint satisfaction is deterministic. Derived metrics (section "Advanced Metrics for Behavior Analysis"): Priority Adherence Ratio PAR = R1/(R1+R2), excluding R3; Constraint Bias CB = (Rc1 - Rc2)/(Rc1 + Rc2) from the NP baseline, normalized to 1 - |CB| for bias resistance; Explicit Conflict Acknowledgement Rate ECAR (statements about contradictions, requests for clarification, or explanations of constraint-selection decisions), with R1ac/R2ac/R3ac reported conditional on acknowledgement (Table 3). There is no task-success or output-quality measure, no LLM judge of quality, and no refusal category (refusals and format failures fold into R3); silent versus announced secondary-following is not reported as a split, only overall R2 and acknowledgement-conditional R2ac. Decoding used provider defaults, not temperature 0: qwen2.5-7b-instruct temp 0.7/top_p 0.8; Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct temp 0.6/top_p 0.9; claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4o-2024-11-20 temp 1.0 (Table 7). No repeated draws, confidence intervals, or seeds are reported.
deep_reads.models_and_tasks: Six models (Table 6): qwen2.5-7b-instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4o-2024-11-20. The societal-hierarchy experiment uses three of them: Qwen-7B, Claude3.5-S, GPT4o-mini. Tasks: 100 IFEval-derived open-ended single-turn writing tasks (resume, resignation email, dialogue, critique, meeting invite, diaper ad, video-game story, Japan blog post, ice-cream pitch, song lyrics, Tang dynasty, etc.), each paired with one of six mutually exclusive formatting constraint pairs; Simple and few-shot-enriched Rich variants. No tool use, no multi-turn, no delegation, no agent harness.
deep_reads.key_numbers: IF baseline (single constraint, no conflict): 74.8-90.8% across models. Average R1 under conflict across the six configuration/data cells (Table 2): Qwen-7B 9.6, Llama-8B 10.1, Llama-70B 16.4, Claude3.5-S 29.9, GPT4o-mini 45.8, GPT4o 40.8 (range quoted as 9.6-45.8%). Best single cells: GPT4o Emphasized/Simple 63.8% R1; Claude3.5-S Emphasized/Rich 47.5%. Larger is not better: Llama-70B 16.4 vs Llama-8B 10.1; GPT4o 40.8 below GPT4o-mini 45.8. ECAR under Pure Separation (Table 3): Qwen-7B 0.1, GPT4o-mini 2.2, Claude3.5-S 2.7, GPT4o 12.0, Llama-8B 15.9, Llama-70B 20.3 (%). Conditional on acknowledgement (R1ac/R2ac/R3ac): Qwen 0.0/100.0/0.0; Llama-8B 20.4/50.3/29.3; Llama-70B 30.7/37.7/31.6; Claude 50.0/31.2/18.8; GPT4o-mini 46.2/0.0/53.8; GPT4o 47.9/0.7/51.4. Shared constraint biases across all six models: lowercase over uppercase, more sentences over fewer, avoiding keywords over including; bias magnitudes often exceed 0.5 (Figure 4). Societal framing PAR vs system/user PAR (Table 4): Qwen-7B 14.4 -> Authority 54.0, Expertise 57.3, Consensus 65.8; Claude3.5-S 23.6 -> 32.4/36.8/62.0; GPT4o-mini 47.5 -> 70.0/73.2/77.8. Ordering effects minimal except Claude under consensus: 85.8 vs 38.2 (Table 8). Dataset: 100 x 6 x 2 = 1,200 data points; Rich constraints 6 x 2 x 100 instances.
deep_reads.overlap: Methodological overlap is real and should be acknowledged: (a) both plant mutually exclusive, programmatically verifiable instruction conflicts between two instruction sources and score the output with deterministic checkers rather than a quality judge; (b) both treat explicit acknowledgement of the conflict as a distinct outcome (their ECAR, and their stripping of acknowledgement text before checking, is the ancestor of our FLAGGED versus announced-DEVIATED distinction, and their R1ac/R2ac is an announced-adhere versus announced-override split); (c) both report that models rarely surface conflicts (ECAR 0.1-20.3%) and that the strongest 2024 models, when they do acknowledge, almost never follow the lower-priority constraint (GPT4o R2ac 0.7%, GPT4o-mini 0.0%), a pattern that rhymes with our pilot in which the frontier model's departures at V2 were announced overrides while the weaker model flagged and kept adhering; (d) both use a two-source hierarchy (their developer/system versus user; our orchestrator brief versus literal assignment) and both find that the hierarchy is not reliably enforced by channel alone; (e) their Rich enrichment is a robustness check against phrasing and length in the same spirit as our length-matched filler arm, though it enriches the constraints themselves rather than adding unrelated context. Their Latent Hierarchical Priors result (authority, expertise, consensus framing beats the system/user role, PAR up to 77.8% vs 47.5%) is orthogonal but bears on our interpretation: a verbatim parent brief at V2 carries "the principal wants X" authority framing, so the V2 effect could act through a latent authority prior rather than through information content, and our filler control removes the length confound but not the authority-framing confound.
deep_reads.differentiation: Four axes, each sufficient on its own. (1) Unit of analysis: Control Illusion is a single LLM in a single-turn chat with two roles; ours is a worker sub-agent inside an orchestrator-worker stack, and their text contains no orchestrator, worker, sub-agent, sibling, ledger, or multi-agent construct at all. Their Limitation section explicitly places "agentic behaviors" outside the evaluation. (2) Independent variable: they vary WHERE a fixed conflict sits (system vs user, three configurations) or HOW it is socially framed; they never vary HOW MUCH of a higher-level principal's context the model sees. Their system message contains only the constraint, the constraint plus the task, or the constraint plus one emphasis sentence; there is no analogue of V1 (one-sentence parent objective), V2 (verbatim parent brief), V3 (sibling mandates), V4 (orchestrator ledger), or V5 (peer-polling tool), and no graded dose-response. (3) Polarity of the dependent variable: they score obedience to the designated-primary (higher-authority) constraint as success, so following the system-level content is the correct behaviour; we score adherence to the literal assignment, so acting on the visible parent brief beyond the assignment is DEVIATED, announced or silent. The same surface behaviour (model follows the higher-level content) is R1 success for them and a deviation for us. (4) Outcome taxonomy and sampling: their three-way R1/R2/R3 plus an LLM-classified ECAR folds refusals and format failures into R3 and never reports silent-versus-announced secondary-following; ours separates ADHERED, FLAGGED, DEVIATED announced vs silent, FAILED_FORMAT, FAILED_BUDGET, FAILED_INCOHERENT, REFUSED. They sample once at provider-default temperatures (0.6-1.0) with no seeds or intervals; we use three draws at temperature 0. Models are 2024-era (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5) versus our 2026 DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and Meta Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor; tasks are IFEval-style writing prompts with formatting constraints versus our worker assignments carrying planted conflict probes inside a hierarchical brief. Position it as the anchor for "hierarchies are not reliably enforced by channel" and as the origin of the conflict-probe plus deterministic-checker plus acknowledgement-rate methodology, then state that it holds the principal's context fixed and scores the opposite polarity.
must_cite_sentences: Abstract: "We find that the widely-adopted system/user prompt separation fails to establish a reliable instruction hierarchy, and models exhibit strong inherent biases toward certain constraint types regardless of their priority designation."

Section "Ineffective Conflict Acknowledgment": "Our analysis of ECAR in Table 3 shows that models rarely acknowledge instruction conflicts, with ECAR ranging from 0.1% (Qwen-7B) to 20.3% (Llama-70B)."

Section "Limitation": "More complex forms of control than formatting constraints, such as safety rules, tone management, or agentic behaviors, remain outside our evaluation as they would require substantially different and more complex evaluation machinery and would shift the scope of the study beyond the core phenomenon examined here."

Section "Ineffective Conflict Acknowledgment" (optional fourth, for the announced-override parallel): "Notably, when GPT models explicitly acknowledge conflicts, they almost never choose to follow the lower-priority constraint."

harnesses.name: Claude Code sub-agents (Agent tool; fork; SubagentStart hooks; --append-subagent-system-prompt)
harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: NONE (fresh, isolated context window). Parent task: only what the orchestrator writes into the delegation prompt (a 'Task message'). Siblings: names only, via a 'sibling roster' system reminder (requires v2.1.206+, only when the subagent has SendMessage and at least one other agent is named); no sibling mandates or outputs. Shared transcript: none; only the subagent's final result returns to the parent. Also receives its own system prompt, all CLAUDE.md levels, a git-status snapshot, and preloaded skills. Exception: a FORK subagent inherits the entire parent conversation (system prompt, tools, model, message history) = full-visibility arm.
harnesses.knob: (1) Delegation prompt text written by the parent (the only channel for parent objective/task). (2) `fork` subagent type via the Agent tool / `/subtask` command (v2.1.212+; `/fork` on v2.1.161-2.1.211): flips to full inheritance of the parent conversation. (3) Frontmatter fields: `prompt`/markdown body (system prompt), `skills` (preload), `memory` (persistent scope), `tools`/`disallowedTools` (e.g. include `SendMessage` to expose the sibling roster; omit `Agent` to stop nesting). (4) `--append-subagent-system-prompt` (headless mode) appends text to every non-fork subagent system prompt, nested included. (5) `SubagentStart` / `SubagentStop` hooks in settings.json, matcher = agent_type; hook input carries `agent_id`, `agent_type`. (6) `SendMessage` to `main` or named siblings for live peer contact (V5-like) and resuming completed subagents. (7) `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` (default three layers).
harnesses.quote: Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read. [...] A fork is a subagent that inherits the entire conversation so far instead of starting fresh. This drops the input isolation that subagents otherwise provide: a fork sees the same system prompt, tools, model, and message history as the main session [...] In non-interactive mode, pass --append-subagent-system-prompt to append your text to the end of every subagent's system prompt, nested subagents included, apart from a forked subagent, which reuses the conversation's own prompt.
harnesses.notes: Doc enumerates the non-fork initial context verbatim: system prompt, Task message, CLAUDE.md hierarchy, git status, preloaded skills, sibling roster. Sibling roster is a snapshot at start (later-named agents absent) and lists names only; it maps to the paper's V3-lite (sibling identities without mandates). Output style and auto memory never reach a non-fork subagent. The hooks page does not document `additionalContext` injection for SubagentStart, so hooks are a lifecycle/side-effect knob, not a documented context-injection knob. Fork skips tool filters and receives the exact parent tool pool; at depth limit a fork keeps `Agent` but it errors. Resumed subagents retain full own history. Nesting default: up to three layers; only the top-level subagent's summary reaches the main conversation.

harnesses.name: OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs (input_filter, handoff_input_filter, nest_handoff_history) and agents-as-tools (Agent.as_tool)
harnesses.default_visibility: HANDOFF: the receiving agent sees the ENTIRE prior conversation history (parent task, all prior items including tool calls) = full transcript visibility. AGENTS-AS-TOOLS: the nested agent run does NOT inherit the parent's conversation state; it receives only the tool-call `input` string (default schema `{"input": "..."}`) = instruction-only visibility. Siblings: not visible in either mode unless present in shared history (handoff) or explicitly passed.
harnesses.knob: Handoffs: `handoff(..., input_filter=fn)` per-handoff (takes/returns `HandoffInputData` with `input_history`, `pre_handoff_items`, `new_items`, `run_context`; per-handoff filter takes precedence); `RunConfig.handoff_input_filter` (global default filter, default None); `RunConfig.nest_handoff_history` (default False, opt-in beta compaction of prior history into assistant summary segments) with per-handoff `nest_handoff_history` override; `agents.extensions.handoff_filters.remove_all_tools` strips tool items. Agents-as-tools: `Agent.as_tool(tool_name, tool_description, custom_output_extractor=..., parameters=...)`; pass the same `session` to parent and nested runs to share client-managed history.
harnesses.fetched_at: 2026-09-03T07:01:28Z (handoffs, tools); 2026-09-03T07:03:42Z (ref/handoffs, ref/run_config)
harnesses.quote: Handoffs: "When a handoff occurs, it's as though the new agent takes over the conversation, and gets to see the entire previous conversation history." input_filter docstring: "A function that filters the inputs that are passed to the next agent. By default, the new agent sees the entire conversation history." Agents as tools: "The state options configure the nested agent run started by the tool call; the parent run's conversation state is not inherited automatically." RunConfig.nest_handoff_history: "Opt-in beta: compact prior run history into ordered assistant summary segments while preserving lossless message items in their original positions. This is disabled by default while we stabilize nested handoffs; set to True to enable the compacted transcript behavior."
harnesses.notes: The same SDK ships both extremes: handoff = full transcript (V4-like, transcript includes orchestrator reasoning items), agents-as-tools = instruction only (V0/V1 depending on what the orchestrator writes into `input`). input_filter is the native dose knob for handoffs; `remove_all_tools` is the shipped filter. Handoffs stay within a single run; input guardrails apply only to the first agent. Server-managed conversations automatically disable nest_handoff_history with a warning. `custom_output_extractor` shapes what returns to the orchestrator, not what the worker sees.

harnesses.name: LangGraph subgraphs and state schemas (plus LangChain supervisor/subagents-as-tools pattern)
harnesses.default_visibility: Subgraph added directly with `add_node`: sees exactly the parent state keys it shares (schema intersection); keys private to the subgraph are invisible to the parent and vice versa. Subgraph invoked inside a node function (different schemas): sees only what the wrapper function passes. Task-mode and single-turn-mode sub-agents (Python/Go v2.0.0) run in an isolated session branch: "each agent only sees events from its own branch when building context for AI model calls, and cannot see what its peer agents are doing" (collaboration page); ParallelAgent likewise: "There is no automatic sharing of conversation history or state between these branches" (parallel-agents page). Siblings: visible by name/description as transfer targets; sibling work visible only through shared session events (chat mode) or session.state keys (output_key, temp:/user:/app: prefixes). Shared ledger: session.state; "When a parent agent calls a sub-agent ... it passes its InvocationContext to the sub-agent ... the same temp: state" (sessions/state page). Returned to parent: Sub-agent (transfer): no return to parent by default; "the responsibility of answering the user is completely transferred to Agent B. Agent A is effectively out of the loop" (chat mode); task/single-turn modes return control automatically to the originating agent. AgentTool: "Agent B's answer is passed back to Agent A, which then summarizes the answer and generates a response to the user"; skip_summarization=True (Python/TS; skipSummarization in Java/Kotlin) bypasses the LLM summarization so the raw final response is the tool result; state/artifact changes are forwarded to the parent context (custom-agents page). Returned to parent: C#: WorkflowOutputEvent carrying the full conversation history (List<ChatMessage>). Siblings or ledger: Siblings fully visible (every broadcast response lands in every participant's session). No separate ledger: the synchronized conversation history is the ledger. harnesses.name: smolagents managed agents (managed_agents=[...])
harnesses.default_visibility: Instruction-only. The managed agent is called like a tool with a `task` string (plus optional `additional_args` dict) and runs with its own AgentMemory; it receives only the managed_agent.task template: "You're a helpful agent named '{{name}}'. You have been submitted this task by your manager. --- Task: {{task}} --- You're helping your manager solve a wider task..." (code_agent.yaml). It does not see the manager's memory, the user's original request, or sibling agents. The template's 'wider task' sentence is a bare hierarchical cue without content. The isolation is still not stated as a sentence in the reference docs; it follows from the API (run(task), own AgentMemory) and the template's interpolating only {{name}} and {{task}}. Returned to parent: The worker's final_answer, wrapped in managed_agent.report ("Here is the final answer from your managed agent '{{name}}': {{final_answer}}"), lands in the manager's memory as a tool observation. The task template forces a three-part final_answer (short outcome, extremely detailed outcome, additional context) and warns that anything not passed to final_answer is lost. provide_run_summary=True appends a run summary. return_full_result (default False, on __init__ and run()) returns a RunResult object instead of the bare final answer. Siblings or ledger: Siblings: not visible to a managed agent. The manager sees its managed agents as callable team members listed in its system prompt (name + description; the prompt tells the manager 'Since this team member is a real human, be as detailed and verbose as necessary'). No shared ledger: each agent has its own AgentMemory.
harnesses.quote: Managed agents that the agent can call.
harnesses.knob: Manager-authored `task` string and `additional_args` dict per call; MultiStepAgent(name=, description=, managed_agents=[...], provide_run_summary=bool, return_full_result=bool, instructions=, prompt_templates=PromptTemplates(managed_agent=ManagedAgentPromptTemplate(task=..., report=...))); planning_interval; max_steps; final_answer_checks.

harnesses.name: eve (eve.dev) subagents: root built-in `agent` tool copies and declared subagents under agent/subagents/<id>/
harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: none. Every subagent (root copy, declared local, remote) "starts with fresh conversation history and fresh state"; the tool input comment reads "message: string; // all context the child needs; it never sees the parent's history" and "The parent packs message with everything the child needs, since the child never sees the parent's history." Parent task reaches the child only through `message`. Root copy inherits the root's instructions, connections, auth, and sandbox and "receives the same tools except for the root-only `agent` and `Workflow`"; a declared subagent "inherits nothing from the root's authored slots". State (defineState) is fresh for both kinds. Returned to parent: Asynchronous: "each call returns { status: \"working\", taskId, agentId }, then task notifications wake the parent with updates or the final result" (built-in copy) and, for declared/remote subagents, "task notifications wake the parent with updates, completion, failure, or cancellation." Only the child's answer (or structured output when outputSchema is set) returns; no child transcript. A child parks after answering, keeping its session and history alive for continuation by agentId. Siblings or ledger: Children: no sibling visibility documented (each subagent is a separate model-visible tool to the parent; nothing is injected into a child beyond `message`). Parent side: a new framework-injected `[Agents]` note with an `<agents>` block lists each parked child's agentId, name, and latest status, appended only when the set of parked children changes; this is a parent-visible child roster/ledger, not something children see. Shared sandbox (root copies) makes file writes mutually visible.

harnesses.name: GitHub Copilot: coding agent (cloud) and Copilot CLI custom agents/subagents (built-in explore, task, general-purpose, code-review, research, rubber-duck; /delegate to coding agent; Copilot SDK custom agents)
harnesses.default_visibility: COPILOT CLI SUBAGENTS: parent conversation: separate context window; what is passed in is not stated. 'The main Copilot agent can run them as subagents with a separate context window' so the agent 'can focus on a specific subtask without cluttering the context window of the main agent'; the work is 'carried out using a subagent, which is a temporary agent spun up to complete the task, with its own context window'. Delegation is model-chosen ('The AI model being used by the CLI can choose to delegate a task to a subsidiary subagent process') or user-directed (/agent, mention, --agent=). Copilot SDK page: 'The sub-agent runs with its own prompt and restricted tool set' in 'an isolated context'; 'sub-agents do not inherit skills from the parent'. COPILOT CODING AGENT (cloud): NO sub-agent mechanism documented. It is a single session that receives the task (issue/prompt), repository content, custom instructions and MCP servers; 'By default, Copilot can only access context in the repository specified when you start a task.' /delegate from the CLI sends only the prompt plus a checkpoint commit of unstaged changes to a new branch; no CLI conversation context is documented as transferred. Reading: CLI subagents V0/V1-by-prose (channel unspecified); coding agent is a top-level worker, not a sub-agent. Returned to parent: Summary by design, documented per built-in agent: the task agent 'returns a brief summary on success, and full output on failure, keeping the main context clean'; other agents' return shape not specified. SDK: outputs are incorporated into the parent's response plus lifecycle events with token/tool metrics. Coding agent / /delegate: a draft pull request and a session link ('Copilot will provide a link to the pull request and agent session on GitHub'); session logs record every step. Siblings or ledger: Not documented. No mechanism for CLI subagents to see each other or share state; SDK page says each runs in an isolated context. Coding agent has no siblings (single session per task).

'A subagent shares tools and codebase context with the parent, but operates in its own conversation chain -- it does not inherit the parent's conversation history.' Parent task: the spawn prompt only. Nesting off by default ('subagents cannot spawn their own subagents') unless a custom profile sets max-nesting. MANAGED DEVINS (cloud, coordinator pattern): each child is a full Devin 'running in its own isolated VM'; the coordinator launches 'child sessions with specific prompts, playbooks, tags, and ACU limits' and can 'send follow-up instructions or clarifications to running sessions'. When a subagent finishes, the parent agent reads the result and summarizes the key findings and actions for you' (the parent model reads the result; read_subagent tool exists). Managed Devins are isolated VMs with their own session links; the coordinator monitors status, todos and PRs via the Agents tab, but no child-to-child visibility or shared ledger is described. harnesses.name: OpenHands Software Agent SDK sub-agent delegation (TaskToolSet task tool with register_agent and file-based agents; legacy DelegateTool spawn/delegate) and microagents (legacy .openhands/microagents/, now skills)
harnesses.default_visibility: TASKTOOLSET (verified): parent conversation: NONE. 'The agent calls the task tool with a prompt and a sub-agent type'; the TaskManager 'creates (or resumes) a sub-agent conversation', so a new task starts a fresh sub-agent conversation whose only input is the prompt; resuming by task_id 'reloads the full conversation history' of that sub-agent (its own, not the parent's). Execution: 'Each sub-agent runs synchronously — the parent blocks until the sub-agent finishes and returns its result.' DELEGATETOOL (legacy, docs page now 404): per the official example, 'a main agent delegates tasks to sub-agents for parallel processing. Each sub-agent runs independently and returns its results to the main agent'. MICROAGENTS are NOT sub-agents: they are prompt snippets, now 'skills'; 'Both the legacy .openhands/skills/ and .openhands/microagents/ directories remain supported, but use .agents/skills/ for new skills'; general skills 'are always loaded as part of the context', keyword skills 'are only loaded when a prompt includes one of the trigger words', and 'Skills guide the agent's behavior; they do not grant permissions or install dependencies by themselves.' Reading: V0/V1-by-prose; microagents are a static-instruction confound like AGENTS.md. Returned to parent: Final response only, as a TaskObservation with task_id, subagent, status ('completed' or 'error') and text ('The sub-agent's response (or error message)'); the sub-agent conversation 'is saved to disk for potential resumption' but is not returned. DelegateTool likewise returns each sub-agent's results for the main agent to consolidate. Siblings or ledger: Not documented: each sub-agent has its own persisted conversation; no sibling visibility, shared state, or ledger primitive is described. TaskToolSet is 'designed for sequential blocking tasks'; parallelism comes from the LLM issuing multiple task calls, with no cross-task channel.

harnesses.name: Roo Code Orchestrator mode / Boomerang tasks (new_task tool, attempt_completion result)
harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: NONE. Each subtask runs in complete isolation with its own conversation history and does not automatically inherit the parent's context. Parent task: only what the orchestrator writes into the `message` parameter of `new_task` ("Via the initial instructions provided when the subtask is created"). The subtask also inherits certain workspace and extension configurations (mode, settings) from the parent, not transcript. Instruction-only default (V0/V1 by prose). Returned to parent: Summary only: "The parent task resumes with only the summary of the subtask", delivered via the `result` parameter of the subtask's `attempt_completion` call (internally `finishSubTask()`); the subtask's transcript never enters the parent context. Siblings or ledger: Siblings: not visible. Execution is sequential: "Parent tasks are paused during subtask execution and resumed when the subtask completes", so there are never concurrent siblings to see; a later subtask sees an earlier one's work only if the orchestrator pastes the returned summary into its message. No shared ledger or peer-status tool is documented.
harnesses.quote: It does not automatically inherit the parent's context.
harnesses.knob: (1) `new_task(mode, message, todos?)`: `message` is the only parent-to-child context channel. harnesses.default_visibility: No sub-agent or delegation primitive. WorkflowAgent is a single durable agent loop run inside a workflow; "DurableAgent is deprecated. Use AI SDK's WorkflowAgent for new durable agents." Neither the AI guide, the WorkflowAgent page, the DurableAgent reference, nor the workflows-and-steps foundations page mentions subagents, multi-agent, or child workflows. A 'worker' would be an ordinary step: "Parameters are passed by value, not by reference", so a step sees exactly the arguments the workflow function passes. Returned to parent: Step return value (by value) to the workflow function; WorkflowAgent returns `result.output` and `result.messages` to its caller. Siblings or ledger: None. Steps can run concurrently via `Promise.all` but share nothing except what the workflow function returns and re-passes; `runtimeContext`/`toolsContext` are in-process agent state, not a cross-agent ledger.

harnesses.name: OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs (input_filter, handoff_input_filter, nest_handoff_history, handoff_history_mapper) and agents-as-tools (Agent.as_tool)
harnesses.default_visibility: Handoff: the receiving agent sees the entire previous conversation history ('it's as though the new agent takes over the conversation'); handoff() keeps the specific destination and 'the receiving agent still sees the conversation history unless you change it with an input_filter'. Agents-as-tools: the nested run receives only the tool-call input (default schema one string field `input`, or a structured `parameters` schema); 'the parent run's conversation state is not inherited automatically'. Returned to parent: Handoff: nothing returns to a parent agent, control transfers ('Handoffs stay within a single run'); the run result is the final agent's output. Agents-as-tools: the nested agent's final output is returned as the tool result to the orchestrator; `custom_output_extractor` reshapes it (e.g. extract a JSON payload); `on_stream` surfaces nested events. The nested transcript is not placed into the parent's conversation unless the same `session` is shared. Siblings or ledger: Handoff: siblings are visible only insofar as their items already sit in the shared history (tool calls, prior handoff items) that the new agent inherits. Agents-as-tools: no sibling visibility; nested runs are independent unless the developer passes the same `session` to parent and nested runs ('To share client-managed history between the parent and nested runs, explicitly pass the same session to both'). No ledger or peer-status primitive.

harnesses.default_visibility: Instruction-only. The manager sees its managed agents as callable team members listed in its system prompt (name + description; the prompt tells the manager 'Since this team member is a real human, be as detailed and verbose as necessary'). Claude launches a teammate 'when it calls the Agent tool with a name while agent teams are enabled', so the spawn prompt is the Agent tool's `prompt` field. Teammates from a subagent definition get its body appended to the default system prompt (in-process) or in place of it (split pane); `skills` and (in-process) `mcpServers` fields are ignored and loaded from project/user settings instead. Messages arriving over SendMessage are labelled as coming 'from another Claude session, not from you', and a relayed approval claim is treated as untrusted. Requires an interactive session: with -p or the Agent SDK 'Claude doesn't spawn teammates, and a subagent that Claude names runs as an ordinary subagent'. Teammates inherit the lead's permission mode and effort level; plan-mode teammates work read-only until the lead session auto-approves their plan ('without the lead reviewing it'). Returned to parent: Final answer only, via an idle notification: 'when a teammate finishes and stops, it automatically notifies the lead and includes its final answer in the notification. A teammate whose turn ends on an API error notifies the lead that it failed and includes the error text.' Messages between agents are 'delivered automatically to recipients. The lead doesn't need to poll for updates.' Shutdown requests can be approved or rejected 'with an explanation'. Teammate transcripts are visible to the human (agent panel, Enter opens the transcript; split panes) but there is no documented path for the lead model to read a teammate transcript. Teammate permission prompts surface in the lead session for the human. Siblings or ledger: Highest sibling visibility of any Claude Code surface, but all opt-in through tools rather than injected context. (1) Shared task list: 'agents that have the Task tools can see task status and claim available work'; states pending/in progress/completed with dependencies; 'Task claiming uses file locking to prevent race conditions when multiple teammates try to claim the same task simultaneously'; stored at ~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/ (persists; team config at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/config.json is removed at session end). Task tools are absent by default on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Mythos 5 unless CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1 or --allowedTools/--tools name them (tools-reference); without them 'an agent coordinates with its team through messages instead of the shared task list'. (2) Roster: the team config 'contains a members array with each member's name and agent ID ... Teammates can read this file to discover other team members'; plus the sub-agents page sibling roster system reminder listing `main` and every named agent (v2.1.206+, only when tools include SendMessage). (3) Mailbox: per-agent JSON at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/inboxes/{agent-name}.json; 'any teammate can message any other by that name'; no broadcast: 'To reach everyone, send one message per recipient.' (4) No nested teams and a teammate's subagents run foreground only.

harnesses.name: Claude Code dynamic workflows (Workflow tool; agent()/pipeline()/parallel() script runtime; /deep-research; ultracode)
harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: NONE, and no fork option. Each agent() call spawns an ordinary subagent whose only task input is the prompt string the script composes: 'A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once'; 'The workflow runtime executes the script in an isolated environment, separate from your conversation. Intermediate results stay in script variables instead of landing in Claude's context.' The bundled workflow-authoring reference (loaded this run, v2.1.248+) adds: 'Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data.' Whether the worker sees the parent objective, sibling results, or a ledger is entirely a property of the script text: prior agent() results are plain variables that the script may or may not interpolate into later prompts. agent() options: label, phase, schema (forces a StructuredOutput tool call), model, effort ('low'..'max'), isolation:'worktree', agentType (custom subagent type from the same registry as the Agent tool, whose system prompt then applies). Workers are subagents, so the sub-agents page's startup list applies (own system prompt, delegation prompt, CLAUDE.md hierarchy, git-status snapshot, preloaded skills); the prompt-caching section confirms same-prefix agents share 'the same tools-and-system-prompt prefix' keyed by model, effort, agent type, tools, output schema and working directory. Workflow agents reach session MCP tools through ToolSearch. No mid-run user input: 'Only agent permission prompts can pause a run.' Returned to parent: agent() 'resolves to' the subagent's final text as a string, or the schema-validated object; 'An agent() call resolves to null if you stop it mid-run or it hits an unrecoverable API error' (pipeline keeps the null; parallel never rejects). The script's own return value is the single thing that reaches the conversation: 'Claude's context holds only the final answer'; the SDK entry says the tool 'returns one consolidated result'. The runtime records every agent's result for resume (journal.jsonl in the run's transcript directory, per the authoring reference) and the human can drill into any agent in /workflows 'to read its prompt, recent tool calls, and result'. Claude receives the persisted script path when the run starts. Siblings or ledger: None injected. The comparison table lists 'Where intermediate results live: Script variables' for workflows versus 'A shared task list' for agent teams and 'Claude's context window' for subagents. Siblings share only a prompt cache, not content: 'Agents in the same run can read each other's prompt cache', with all-but-first agents in a fan-out held up to CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS (5000 ms default). Cross-item context exists only when the script builds a barrier (parallel) and feeds results into later prompts, e.g. the adversarial-verify and judge-panel patterns in the authoring reference. Nested workflow() calls share the run's concurrency cap, agent counter and budget, one level deep.

harnesses.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio multi-agent: child agents (inline) and connected agents (Copilot Studio, A2A, Foundry, Fabric, M365 Agents SDK) under the standard harness generative orchestration
harnesses.default_visibility: Two different defaults. CHILD AGENT: full parent context, not switchable: 'A child agent, by contrast, always receives the parent's context' (patterns page) and 'It runs inside the parent and always receives the parent's conversation context, with no setting to exclude it' (context-design page); 'By default, a child agent receives a natural language task to accomplish from the main agent when the agent calls it.' CONNECTED AGENT: the 'Pass conversation history to this agent' checkbox, 'enabled by default'; clearing it 'limits the information being passed to the agent to just the explicit task that the main agent wants the other agent to complete' so the agent 'works only from the inputs the parent sends, not the full conversation.' The context-design table gives the subagent's active context as 'Its initial request, plus parent-provided inputs and any included parent context, within its own orchestration layer context'; 'The orchestration layer also passes a longer conversation context to components such as knowledge and to subagents without explicit configuration.' Subagents are not told they are orchestrated: 'Subagents don't inherently know they're part of an orchestration. Without explicit guidance, they behave as standalone agents and send messages directly to the user.' Instruction precedence: 'The platform injects system-level instructions by using strong language (MUST, DO NOT, NEVER). Instructions written with soft language ... lose priority when they conflict.' Recommended reinforcement: put 'Return your findings only. Don't reply to the user.' in the delegated task text as well as in the subagent's instructions. Parent cannot stop a running subagent: 'Telling the parent agent, "You're the only agent that talks to the user," doesn't work.' The GitHub Copilot harness differs: the parent is the sole communicator and 'Connected agent messages pass through the parent's AI layer at every turn.' Returned to parent: Child agent: 'When it completes its task, it returns a natural language summary of what happened during its execution' plus any maker-defined typed outputs. Generic contract: 'The parent can't see the subagent's exchange with the user and learns the result only through the defined outputs and implicit response'; 'Only two types of information return' (explicit outputs and implicit context); topic variables and multi-turn exchanges inside a subagent stay hidden unless returned. Connected agents have separate transcripts ('you have separate transcripts for it'), correlated by telemetry identifiers. Recommended output contract: answered (Boolean), scopedRequest, interactionSummary, findings, openQuestions. 'Citations might not always be maintained when passing outputs back.' After running options let the parent respond immediately using the child's outputs as context. Siblings or ledger: Not stated for subagent-to-subagent visibility; nothing describes a child or connected agent seeing another's context or outputs. The orchestration layer holds 'component descriptions, input descriptions, output descriptions, plan state, implicit responses' and routes by description; multiple child agents can fire on the same activity in creation or Priority order. Guidance assumes non-overlapping knowledge per subagent because 'one subagent finds the answer first' and the other duplicates or skips. Connected-agent nesting is limited: an agent that has connected agents cannot itself be a connected agent of another main agent.
harnesses.quote: A child agent, by contrast, always receives the parent's context.

It does not communicate with the user directly'; 'Each sub-agent has a fully independent context window. It can only see the task description explicitly passed by the main Agent and cannot see the main Agent's conversation history.' The Agent tool's required inputs are 'prompt (complete task description) and description (a 3-5 word short summary)'; AgentSwarm launches subagents 'from a shared prompt_template and an items array' where '{{item}}' is substituted per subagent. Objective reaches the worker only if the main agent writes it into the prompt. Experimental full-transcript switch since 0.39.0 (2026-08-27): 'an optional fork parameter to subagent and swarm tools that starts the subagent with a snapshot of the calling agent's conversation history; set KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_SUBAGENT_FORK=1 or subagent_fork = true under [experimental]'. Custom agents delegated as sub-agents 'run without the built-in sub-agent framing ("your final message is the entire handoff")'. Each dispatch is shown to the user as an approval request with the task description unless an allow rule or Ask When Needed mode applies. Tower mode (experimental, 0.39.0+, KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_TOWER=1) is a separate multi-agent orchestration surface whose context policy is not documented on these pages. Returned to parent: Final result only: 'The sub-agent's own intermediate reasoning and tool call records do not flow back; only the final result appears in the main Agent's context.' Background sub-agents deliver 'via a synthetic User message when done'; a sub-agent that finished while background tasks were running 'only reports completion after those tasks settle'. AgentSwarm 'waits for all subagents to finish, and returns an aggregated report'; a timed-out subagent 'is aborted and marked as failed in the aggregated report'. Full sub-agent history is persisted locally for the human, not the model: each sub-agent's 'wire.jsonl file that records prompts, message history, and final state'. Existing sub-agents can be resumed (resume / resume_agent_ids). Siblings or ledger: None. 'Multiple sub-agents can run in parallel without interfering with each other'; no inter-sub-agent messaging, shared task list, or ledger is documented for the Agent or AgentSwarm tools (the community thread kimi-cli discussion #969 records 'Subagents cannot communicate with each other'). The AgentSwarm aggregated report goes to the caller only. Recursion is bounded: 'The three built-in sub-agents cannot dispatch further sub-agents'; 'By default a custom agent inherits the built-in delegation allowlist (coder, explore, plan), whose members cannot dispatch further either, so delegation chains always terminate and unbounded recursive spawning is impossible without an explicit opt-in'; a custom agent opts in with an explicit `subagents` allowlist (`*` allows every type); changelog 0.35.0 (2026-08-12) 'Fix coder subagents spawning further subagents by default.'

harnesses.name: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) subagent seam: spawn, fork, acp providers via dsh-tool-subagent; dsh-tool-subagent-control (send_message, interrupt_agent, list_agents)
harnesses.default_visibility: Provider-dependent, and the model-facing tool wording is derived from the provider's `inheritsParentContext` flag. spawn (in-process, default example in the tool README): 'The child starts with an empty conversation, so a task prompt must stand alone'; 'The fresh child receives the task content verbatim as its only user message in a new empty conversation, with the parent provider, model, reasoning effort, output-token limit, and working directory by default'; 'No parent conversation message is included'. Tool description the model sees under spawn/acp: 'The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation.' fork (in-process): 'seeds each child with the parent's completed conversation turns: the child sees every finished turn and none of the in-flight one'; the seed is 'a balanced completed-turn prefix of the parent's log — the parent's events up to and including its last turn/end'; 'The seed is captured once at start; later parent turns never reach the child'; the tool wording becomes 'it does not see the current in-flight turn'. acp (out-of-process, any ACP-compatible agent): 'the child gets its own runtime, session, model configuration, and tools'; 'the parent supplies only the task and the working directory'; 'ACP reads only its cwd'. Codex and Claude Code product providers also exist (dsh-subagent-codex, dsh-subagent-claude-code) and, like ACP, 'reject agentOptions before starting their transports'. The subsystem doc states the flag values outright: '`inheritsParentContext` describes only conversation seeding (`fork`: true; `spawn` and `acp`: false)'. Parent task: nothing beyond the delegation `prompt` (SubagentStartRequest.prompt = 'Content delivered as the child's user message'); no objective or brief field exists in the schema (`description` is a 3-5 word display label). Returned to parent: Final output only. Tool description: 'The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps.' One-shot `SubagentResult` carries `output` (final assistant text), optional `structured` (when `outputSchema` was satisfied), `stopReason` (completed \| max-tokens \| refusal \| aborted \| error) and an optional sanitized `diagnostic` capped at 4096 UTF-8 bytes from which providers 'remove tool inputs, file contents, environment values, credentials, and raw protocol payloads'; a non-completed stop reason maps to an `isError` tool result rather than partial success. ACP: 'The parent receives only the child's final answer or a safe error — no intermediate messages or tool traffic crosses the boundary.' Background one-shot returns 'started background subagent job <id>' collected via `job_output`; continuable returns 'started subagent <childId>' and one settlement notice when the child's Activation ends. Observers (not the parent model) get paired `subagent/start` / `subagent/end` events and can enumerate children via `listChildren` / `listDescendants` without loading an agent. Siblings or ledger: No shared ledger. `send_message` is strictly adjacent: 'permits only a direct parent or direct continuable child'; 'Siblings, ancestors beyond one edge, self-targets, stale Agent objects, and one-shot children are rejected.' Delivered messages are framed 'Agent <sender-id> sent a message:' and 'provenance records the sender but grants no authority'. `list_agents` (separately loadable `/list-agents` plugin) shows the caller's continuable children with status running/idle/ready, not siblings. In-process children 'get a new flat scope rather than inheriting parent registrations'; one-shot children share the parent's working directory (ACP shares only cwd).
harnesses.quote: Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation.
harnesses.knob: (1) Provider choice per mounted tool instance (`provider: spawn \| fork \| acp \| codex \| claude-code \| dsh-sdk`); several instances can coexist with distinct `toolName`s (the catalog shows `subagent` and `subagent_fork` side by side). (2) `maxDepth` (default 3; 0 forbids delegation; `'provider-managed'` for out-of-process providers); depth is durable in `SessionHeader.delegationDepth`, child = parent + 1, and cold resume cannot lower it. (3) `persona` (per-child system-prompt section that shadows `deployment:persona`), `toolFilter` (allow/deny global tools; they 'vanish from the child's prompt AND refuse to execute'), `agentOptions` (provider/model/reasoningEffort/maxTokens), `outputSchema` (structured result via a forced capture tool), each gated by a provider capability flag and rejected loudly when unsupported (ACP supports none). (4) `backgroundMode: one-shot \| continuable` and `enableRunInBackground`; continuable children are durable sessions the parent can message. (5) `modelSelectionSettings` exposes `provider`/`model`/`reasoning_effort` fields plus `list_subagent_models`. (6) ACP provider: `command`, `args`, `cwd`, `permission: reject \| allow`, credential-scrubbed `env`. No knob passes the parent's objective or a brief separately from the prompt; the only transcript knob is the provider switch to fork.

harnesses.name: Hermes Agent (Nous Research) delegate_task subagents (leaf / orchestrator roles, batch mode, worktree isolation, /review reviewer)
harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: NONE. 'Subagents start with a completely fresh conversation. They have zero knowledge of the parent's conversation history, prior tool calls, or anything discussed before delegation. The subagent's only context comes from the goal and context fields the parent agent populates when it calls delegate_task.' Parent task: only what the parent writes into `goal` (required task description) and `context` (required, 'Full context the subagent needs'); the page's BAD/GOOD example shows `goal="Fix the error"` failing because the child cannot resolve 'the error'. 'The subagent receives a focused system prompt built from your goal and context, instructing it to complete the task and provide a structured summary of what it did, what it found, any files modified, and any issues encountered.' Exception to isolation: the repo context files (see static_instruction_confound). The separate `/review` reviewer 'inherits the primary agent's working context: any skills the primary agent had loaded ... are named in its briefing with an instruction to load them'. Each child has 'their own terminal sessions'; by default children share the parent's working directory. Returned to parent: 'only its final summary enters the parent's context'. The child is instructed to return a structured summary (what it did, what it found, files modified, issues). The tool result carries `status` (`failed` plus a single most-informative error line on failure), timeout metadata (`timeout_seconds`, `timed_out_after_seconds`, `timeout_phase`), a `worktree` block when isolation is on (path, branch, commits, dirty status), and `live_transcripts` paths. Top-level calls run in the background: 'Hermes returns a handle immediately so the conversation can continue, then posts the result back as a new message'; batch results are 'sorted by task index to match input order regardless of completion order'; a stopped child's 'partial result still re-enters the conversation as a normal completion message'. Full child transcripts are written to `<hermes_home>/cache/delegation/live/<delegation_id>/task-<n>.log` (assistant text, thinking, tool calls) for a human or the parent to `tail -f`, i.e. an on-disk ledger the parent could read with a file tool but is not fed by default. Siblings or ledger: No sibling messaging: `send_message` is blocked for children ('no cross-platform side effects'). Batch siblings run in a ThreadPoolExecutor and share the working directory unless `worktree_isolation` is on ('children can't clobber each other's edits'). The parent's `list` control returns its live children (subagent_id, goal, status, running_seconds, accepting_steer, live transcript path); children have no such view of each other. The live-transcript log files are the only ledger-like artifact and are readable from the filesystem, including remote terminal backends (Docker/Modal/SSH).
harnesses.quote: Subagents start with a completely fresh conversation.
harnesses.knob: Per call: `goal`, `context`, `max_iterations` (default 50), `role: leaf \| orchestrator` (leaf is default and cannot delegate), `background`, and batch `tasks=[{goal, context}, ...]`. Config `delegation.*`: `max_concurrent_children` (default 3, floor 1, no ceiling; also DELEGATION_MAX_CONCURRENT_CHILDREN), `max_spawn_depth` (default 1 = flat; 'Raise to 2 to allow orchestrator children to spawn leaf grandchildren; 3+ for deeper trees. There is no upper ceiling'), `orchestrator_enabled` (false forces all children to leaf), `worktree_isolation` (default false; each child gets `<repo>/.worktrees/subagent-<id>` on branch `hermes-subagent/subagent-<id>`, 'inspired by Muse Code's --subagent-worktree-isolation'), `model`/`provider`/`api_mode` overrides (empty model = inherit the parent's). `delegate_task does not accept a model-facing toolsets parameter. Blocked in children: `delegate_task` (leaf), `clarify`, `memory`, `send_message`, `cronjob`. Control actions `list`, `steer` (queue a course correction into a running child), `stop`. No knob passes the parent transcript or objective; the parent must author `context`.

Blog: 'The worker model sees only what the delegating model explicitly passes in the task_description. No parent conversation, no prior context, no memory between tasks. Parent task: only what the orchestrating model writes into `task_description` ('Everything the worker needs to complete the task: full context, inputs, constraints, and the expected output format. 'On success the tool result contains the outcome text, the task name, and the model that produced it': `{status: "ok", model, task_name, outcome}`; on failure `{status: "error", task_name, error}` and 'the calling model continues without the outcome'. A completed `openrouter:subagent` output item (new id, same `call_id`) carries `task_name`, `task_description`, `model`, `outcome`; the `response.output_item.added` event for a suspended item is deferred until the spawning call's arguments finish streaming. Siblings or ledger: None. Multiple delegations in one request are independent tasks with 'no memory between tasks'; no messaging, no shared state, no ledger. Blog: 'Each delegation is a clean, isolated unit of work.'

Each subagent sees only the instructions provided by the lead, not the original task description, and subagents can message any other agent and the lead.' N-agent team (peers, N=5 or 10): 'One agent is designated the lead and is responsible for coordination and submitting the final answer if needed, but all agents have identical tools and all see the full task description.' Returned to parent: 'A subagent's final response is delivered to the lead as a message, after which the subagent idles until the lead wakes it with new instructions.' Messages are 'inserted following the recipient's next tool result'. 'For search tasks, only the lead agent's final submission is graded.' Siblings or ledger: Full peer messaging in both harnesses: Send Message 'delivers a message to one or more teammates' and Wait for Message 'blocks sampling until an incoming message arrives'; in the async harness 'subagents can message any other agent and the lead'. harnesses.name: Anthropic Managed Agents multiagent orchestration (coordinator roster, session threads, agent_toolset_20260401) plus the session-log / getEvents() primitive from the engineering post
harnesses.default_visibility: Docs page (unchanged from the existing row): 'each agent runs in its own session thread, a context-isolated event stream with its own conversation history'; 'Tools, MCP servers, and context are not shared'; shared sandbox, filesystem and vault credentials. Engineering post (Apr 08, 2026) adds the architecture behind it: the session is 'a context object that lives outside Claude's context window ... context is durably stored in the session log. The interface, getEvents(), allows the brain to interrogate context by selecting positional slices of the event stream ... pick up from wherever it last stopped reading, rewinding a few events before a specific moment to see the lead up, or rereading context before a specific action.' The post frames getEvents() as the brain's window onto its own session log (the harness uses it to rebuild context after a crash or compaction); it does not say a child thread can call getEvents() on the coordinator's primary thread, and the docs page exposes no agent-facing tool for reading another thread's events. Per-thread event streams (`/v1/sessions/{session_id}/threads/{thread_id}/stream`, same `event_deltas[]` parameter) are a client API, and 'a child thread's previews never appear on the session-level stream'. Returned to parent: Unchanged: reports or questions as messages ('On the primary thread, an agent sent a report or question to the coordinator. Includes from_session_thread_id, from_agent_name, and content'). The primary thread is 'a condensed view of all activity across all threads. You don't see the full activity from subagents, but you do see the start and end of their work, and blocking events such as tool permission requests.' 'Critical events are proxied to the primary thread'; the full child transcript is reachable only by the client via the thread's own event stream ('to watch a subagent live, open its own thread stream'). Engineering post: the session log 'sits outside the harness', so the durable record of every thread exists server-side regardless of what the coordinator's model sees. Siblings or ledger: Unchanged: coordinator has `list_agents` and `send_to_agent`; nothing documents roster agents seeing or messaging each other; the advisor is reachable only from the primary thread ('Roster agents cannot'). harnesses.name: Claude Code auto mode classifier at subagent handoffs (addition to the existing Claude Code sub-agents row)
harnesses.default_visibility: Not a visibility change for the worker; the post confirms the existing row's V0 framing from the safety side: 'Inside the subagent, the orchestrator's instruction is the user message, so tasks look fully authorized.' What the classifier itself sees: 'The classifier sees only user messages and the agent's tool calls; we strip out Claude's own messages and tool outputs, making it reasoning-blind by design'; it is a two-stage transcript classifier ('Stage 1 is a fast single-token (yes/no) filter instructed to err toward blocking; if it flags, stage 2 re-evaluates the same input with chain-of-thought reasoning'). Tiering: 'The transcript classifier sees everything else, including shell commands, web fetches, external tool integrations, subagent spawns, filesystem operations outside the project directory.' At delegation: 'The classifier runs at both ends of a subagent handoff: when work is delegated out and when results come back. The outbound check exists because, without it, the transcript classifier that monitors the subagent may not have the full context to know if the task it was given was originally intended by the user ... We catch it at delegation, while it's still recognizable as an agent choice rather than a user request.' Returned to parent: On return the classifier, not the parent model, reads the whole subagent transcript: 'The return check exists because a subagent that was benign at delegation could be compromised mid-run by a prompt injection in content it reads. Before results go back to the orchestrator, the classifier reviews the subagent's full action history. If it flags, we prepend a security warning for the agent that started the subagent rather than discard the results.' So the parent receives the subagent's result plus, when flagged, a prepended warning; the subagent's action history stays with the classifier. Siblings or ledger: Not addressed. The classifier is a per-handoff observer over one subagent's action history; nothing about sibling or ledger visibility.
harnesses.quote: Inside the subagent, the orchestrator's instruction is the user message
harnesses.knob: Auto mode itself (the post positions it as replacing --dangerously-skip-permissions); deny-and-continue semantics when the classifier blocks. Delegation default: agents page 'Allow the agent to delegate tasks to other agents. Default is False.'; hierarchical-process page feature list: 'Delegation Control: Delegation is now disabled by default to give users explicit control.' Manager: 'A manager agent allocates tasks among crew members based on their roles and capabilities'; 'The manager assigns tasks strategically, considering each agent's capabilities and available tools.' Sequential chaining (tasks page): 'the output of one task is automatically relayed into the next one, but you can specifically define what tasks' output ... should be used as context for another task' via Task(context=[...]); 'forward references are rejected so sequential context stays explicit' (JSON crews). harnesses.default_visibility: Parent conversation: NOT STATED.
